pages.title: Owner sessions
pages.description: Everything only the owner can do — accounts, GPU runs, golden data, devices — in three sittings ordered by dependency, with the time and the exact command for each, and free cloud devices instead of owning test phones.
pages.md:
**Run it as a command:** `npm run owner:session -- accounts|gpu|devices` prints each step, runs and verifies it, and records a signed receipt ([Owner session command](/project/owner-session-command/), plan W6.20). It regroups the items below into 14 steps.

Plan W4.7. Gathered 12.11.2026 from `plan.json` → `owner` (15.1–15.18) and the
"## Owner commands" sections of all 300 open pull requests (37 have one).
Every item is either here, with its time and command, or listed under
"Taken off the owner's list" with who does it instead.

**Order:** Session 1 (accounts) first — store verification takes days and
several later steps need its tokens. Session 2 (GPU Mac) and session 3
(devices) can then go in either order. 15.1 (merging) comes last.

Commands that come with an open pull request are written as the script they run (the PR is named next to them), so they work on that PR's branch before it is merged: `node scripts/models-day.mjs` is #443's `models:day`, `bash scripts/pages-deploy.sh` is #484's `pages:deploy`.

## The count

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Plan items 15.1–15.18 | 18 | **11** (−39%): 15.2, 15.10, 15.16 decided; 15.5 and 15.6 deferred (optional); 15.14 and 15.17 run inside 15.3's one command. **10 (−44%)** once BrowserStack approves the open-source plan and an agent runs 15.12's Safari part on BrowserStack Automate |
| All owner items (15.x + PR owner sections, duplicates merged) | 40 | **28** (−30%): 14 PRs' test runs, 3 data downloads and 4 model pins moved to agents |
| Owner time in the 15.x estimates | ≈ 21 h 40 min | ≈ 2 h 10 min (session 1) + ≈ 2 h 55 min attended and ≈ 2 h unattended (session 2) + 5 h 30 min of golden data (2.8, over several days) + ≈ 3 h 35 min (session 3) ≈ 14 h of your time |
| Devices Tal must own for Safari / iOS / Android checks | iPhone, Mac Safari, Android phone | none for Safari/iOS (BrowserStack open-source plan) and Android smoke runs (Firebase Test Lab, no-cost quota); a phone stays needed for share-sheet, widget and Files-app checks |

## Session 1 — accounts, keys and switches (≈ 2 h 10 min, + 20 min for the optional 1.10; any computer)

| # | Item (source) | Time | Command / where |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1.1 | **15.18 (P0)** `VITE_*` secrets that leaked into bundles before #243 | 20 min | `npx vercel@latest env ls` (and Netlify: `netlify env:list`). Any token or key among them: revoke at the provider, create a new one, store it server-side only (`vercel env add  production` without the `VITE_` prefix). | 1.2 | 15.9 remainder: Hugging Face token + golden-set seed | 3 min | `vercel env add HF_TOKEN preview` · `openssl rand -hex 32 \| vercel env add GOLDEN_SEED preview` |
| 1.3 | 15.11 part: dataset terms | 5 min | Logged in to Hugging Face with the `HF_TOKEN` account: accept the terms of `openlanguagedata/flores_plus`; accept Common Voice's dataset terms where 7.1's download fetches it from. |
| 1.4 | W4.28 activation (#481) | 5 min | `gh label create human-reviewed --repo talstilkol/lumen-md --color 0E8A16 --description "A person reviewed the diff after the last commit"` · `gh api -X PUT repos/talstilkol/lumen-md/private-vulnerability-reporting` · secret scanning + push protection: Settings → Code security → enable both (free for public repos; both are off today). |

| 1.7 | W4.27 second host (#484) | 15 min | `npx wrangler@4 login` · `npx wrangler@4 pages project create lumen-md --production-branch main` · `git checkout chore/second-host && npm ci && bash scripts/pages-deploy.sh --prod` |

Git CORS proxy: per 15.4 in the plan. |
| 1.10 | *Optional* — **15.5** Drive and Dropbox OAuth apps (#483); deferred, do it only to offer those two providers | 20 min | Google Cloud Console → OAuth client (Web), redirect `https://lumen-md.vercel.app/oauth/gdrive`, scope `drive.file` · Dropbox App Console → scoped app (App folder), redirect `https://lumen-md.vercel.app/oauth/dropbox` · `vercel env add VITE_GDRIVE_CLIENT_ID production` · `vercel env add VITE_DROPBOX_APP_KEY production` |

## Session 2 — models and data, on the GPU Mac (≈ 2 h 55 min attended + ≈ 2 h unattended; 2.8's golden-set work is 5 h 30 min more, over several days)

Prerequisites: session 1.2–1.3; Ollama installed; a checkout with #443 (`models:day`).

| # | Item (source) | Time | Command |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2.1 | **15.3 + 15.14 + 15.17** real models, browser engines, phase-6 checks; also #449 (tool calls) and #454 (web dictation) | 15 min + ≈ 2 h unattended | `npm ci && node scripts/models-day.mjs check` (install what is ✗) · `node scripts/models-day.mjs` · then push the run folder as it prints (`git switch -c eval/day-<run> && git add -f eval/results/day/<run> && git commit -m "eval: real models day <run> [skip ci]" && git push -u origin HEAD`) |
| 2.2 | DictaLM-3 eval (#379; the agent fills `models/dictalm3.json` from the HF API first) | 20 min | `ollama pull hf.co/dicta-il/DictaLM-3.0-1.7B-Thinking-GGUF && ollama pull qwen3:4b` · `node scripts/dictalm3.mjs eval --size 1.7B` · `node scripts/dictalm3.mjs decide --json eval/results/dictalm3-decision.json` |
| 2.3 | ivrit.ai Whisper on the desktop (#383, W1.17; the agent pins the model first) | 25 min | `brew install whisper-cpp` · download the pinned file to `~/Library/Application Support/app.lumen.editor/whisper/` (URL printed by the pin) · `node scripts/whisper-desktop.mjs wer --split test=<golden>/asr-he/test --model <file>` (targets: WER ≤ 10%, < 10 min per audio hour) |
| 2.4 | Speaker diarization speed (#398; the agent pins both networks) | 15 min | dev build on the M1: transcribe a 1-hour recording, read "RTF" in the console (target < 0.25); `node scripts/meetings/der.mjs --golden <dir> --out der-scores.json` once 2.8's meetings are labelled |
| 2.5 | Literature-review and canvas-draw evals (#438, #404) | 10 min | `ollama pull qwen2.5:7b && LUMEN_EVAL_LIT=1 npx vitest run --config vitest.eval.config.ts src/agents/eval/litReview.eval.ts` · `node scripts/canvas-draw-eval.mjs --model qwen2.5:7b` |
| 2.6 | 15.13 parts on the Mac: local LoRA (6.12), data analyst vs a real model (6.15, 20 golden questions) | 30 min | per the 6.12 / 6.15 PR owner sections (`node scripts/models-day.mjs` covers the data-analyst eval when 6.15 is merged) |
| 2.7 | Your own archives (#482 mail, #478 chats) | 30 min | ~50 old Hebrew `.eml` (windows-1255 / ISO-8859-8) + a Gmail Takeout → ⌘K *Import mail…*; 10 chats (WhatsApp Android + iPhone, Telegram JSON) → ⌘K *Import a WhatsApp or Telegram chat…*; send redacted first lines of anything misread |
| 2.8 | **15.11** your part of the golden sets | 5 h 30 min (split over days) | 20 voice recordings + CC0 consent (30 min — record them once: they also serve #458's voice commands and #398's 5 short meetings, 20 min) · 60 niqqud sentences + 50 error pairs proofread (1 h 30) · 20 image reference descriptions (45 min) · 30 personal queries labelled (1 h) · 30 Hebrew injection attacks (45 min) · 15 photographed pages (20 min) · 50 translations rated (45 min) |
| 2.9 | **15.15** rate the local image descriptions (after 6.6) | 30 min | the rating sheet the 6.6 PR prints, 1–5 per image, 50 images |

## Session 3 — devices and manual checks (≈ 3 h 35 min)

| # | Item (source) | Time | How (free cloud first) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3.1 | **15.12** Safari + W2.8 Hebrew keyboard layout + W4.21 WebKit | 30 min | BrowserStack Live (session 1.6): Safari on macOS and iPhone, open https://lumen-md.vercel.app, run the 15.12 checklist with the Hebrew input source; no device of yours |
| 3.2 | 15.12 Word (RTL) and the automatic update | 30 min | Open the exported `.docx` from #263 in Word, check direction and lists · install build N, publish N+1 as a prerelease (needs 1.5's updater key), *Check for updates* → installs and restarts |
| 3.3 | **15.8** desktop release checks + the native build (#479) + store packages (#423) | 60 min | Mac: `npm ci && npm run tauri:build`; Linux: `sudo apt-get install -y libwebkit2gtk-4.1-dev libgtk-3-dev libayatana-appindicator3-dev librsvg2-dev && cargo check --locked --manifest-path src-tauri/Cargo.toml && npm run tauri:build`; then CSP, Graphviz / Python / OCR, a vault folder, the same vault opened in Obsidian · `node scripts/release.mjs packages` and the `brew audit` / `winget validate` / `flatpak-builder` / `makepkg` lines of #423 on each OS |

- #388 TTS listening test: 5 raters (`node scripts/tts-mos.mjs sheet --raters <5 names>`).

pages.title: Open PR triage
pages.description: One decision table for every open pull request — in main, in a train, superseded, dependabot, or still needed — and the commands that close each category with a comment.
pages.md:
Most pull requests here are stacked: each one is built on the branch of the
one before. When a train (`verify/train`, `verify/train-2`, …) is merged, GitHub
does not mark the PRs inside it as merged, so they stay open. 356 open PRs
hide the few that are really open work (plan W6.21).

`scripts/pr-triage.mjs` sorts every open PR into one category, so the owner
approves a **category** once instead of each PR:

| Category | Rule | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| `in-main` | `git merge-base --is-ancestor <head> origin/main`: every commit of the PR is in main | Close now, with a comment |

  can be reopened.

  different head, so it counts as `needed`, not contained. The script errs

pages.title: Releasing a version
pages.description: One local command builds, signs and checks a release, and with --publish puts it on GitHub Releases with signed desktop updates. No GitHub Actions.
pages.md:
A release is one command on the release owner's computer. GitHub Actions
are not needed.

```bash
npm run release -- 0.2.0-beta.1 --dry-run     # build, sign and check everything; publish nothing
npm run release -- 0.2.0-beta.1 --publish     # the owner: commit, tag, build, sign, push, GitHub release
```

A dry run puts the tree back when it finishes: the version, `CHANGELOG.md` and
`src-tauri/tauri.conf.json` return to what they were. It leaves `release/`
with every asset, plus `release/DRY-RUN.md`, which lists the assets and the
exact commands `--publish` would run.

## What the command does

1. **Preflight.** It lists everything that is missing (a key, a tool, the
   release notes, a clean tree, the `main` branch, `gh auth`), each with the
   command that fixes it. A dry run needs no key. A publish needs every one.
2. **Version and changelog.** It bumps the version in `package.json`,
   `package-lock.json`, `tauri.conf.json`, `Cargo.toml` and the iOS project.
   It writes the `CHANGELOG.md` section from the pull requests merged since
   the last tag: one line per PR, sorted by the type in its title (Added,
   Fixed, Performance, …), with a link to the PR. PR titles come from the
   GitHub API; offline (`--offline`) it uses the merge commits.
3. **Commit and tag** (`--publish` only): `chore(release): X` and `vX`.
4. **The updater.** The committed `tauri.conf.json` carries the placeholder
   `${LUMEN_UPDATER_PUBKEY}`. The release fills in the public key and the
   endpoint on GitHub Releases (stable: `releases/latest/download/latest.json`;
   a beta: the rolling `beta-channel` release). It also turns on signed update
   bundles. The build stops if the key is empty, is still the placeholder or
   is not a minisign key. Afterwards the file goes back to the placeholder.
5. **A reproducible web build.** `repro-check` builds twice with
   `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` and compares every file, then the bundle budget and the
   source-map check run. `lumen-web-vX.tgz` is the same bytes on every machine:
   the files are sorted, the owner and mode are fixed, and the gzip header has
   no time.
6. **Desktop.** `tauri build` runs with `TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY`. The macOS
   update bundle gets its version and architecture in its name.
   `latest.json` is built from the `.sig` files. Every signature is checked
   against the updater key, and the same check must refuse a copy with one
   byte changed.
7. **SBOM.** `sbom.cdx.json` (CycloneDX 1.5) lists every package in
   `package-lock.json` and every crate in `Cargo.lock`. It is built offline.
8. **Release notes.** Hebrew first, then English, from
   `release-notes/<version>.he.md` and `release-notes/<version>.en.md`
   (written by hand, a few lines each), then the full change list and how to
   verify the download.
9. **Checksums.** `SHA256SUMS` lists every asset. It is signed with minisign
   (`SHA256SUMS.minisig`), and so is the SBOM. The whole folder is then
   verified, and a changed `SHA256SUMS` must fail.
10. **Publish** (`--publish` only): `git push origin HEAD vX`, then
    `gh release create`. A beta is a pre-release and is never "latest", so
    stable users never get it. Then `latest.json` is uploaded to the
    `beta-channel` release.

## Options

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| `--dry-run` | the default: nothing is committed, tagged or published |
| `--publish` | the real release (the owner) |
| `--fake-build` | dry run only: stand-in bundles where `node_modules`, Rust or the Tauri CLI are missing; every later step still runs. A publish refuses it. |
| `--no-repro` | one web build instead of two |
| `--no-desktop` | web, SBOM and checksums only |
| `--skip-checks` | no typecheck and no tests before the build |
| `--offline` | PR titles from git, not from the GitHub API |

## Keys (made once, kept by the owner)

| Key | Made with | Used through |
|---|---|---|

```bash
gh release download v0.2.0-beta.1 --repo talstilkol/lumen-md --dir lumen
cd lumen && minisign -Vm SHA256SUMS -p release-key.pub && sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS
```

## Limits

- One `--publish` run uploads the bundles of the machine it runs on: the
  macOS bundles from a Mac. Bundles for Linux and Windows from other
  machines are not added to the same release yet. Until they are, publish
  from the Mac (that gives at least the `.dmg`, the update bundle, its
  signature, the web `.tgz` and the SBOM).

sections.heading: Releasing a version
sections.text: A release is one command on the release owner's computer. GitHub Actions are not needed. A dry run puts the tree back when it finishes: the version, CHANGELOG.md and src-tauri/tauri.conf.json return to what they were. It leaves release/ with every asset, plus release/DRY-RUN.md, which lists the assets and the exact commands --publish would run.

sections.heading: What the command does
sections.text: 1. Preflight. It lists everything that is missing (a key, a tool, the release notes, a clean tree, the main branch, gh auth), each with the command that fixes it. A dry run needs no key. A publish needs every one. 2. Version and changelog. It bumps the version in package.json, package-lock.json, tauri.conf.json, Cargo.toml and the iOS project. It writes the CHANGELOG.md section from the pull requests merged since the last tag: one line per PR, sorted by the type in its title (Added, Fixed, Performance, …), with a link to the PR. PR titles come from the GitHub API; offline (--offline) it uses the merge commits. 3. Commit and tag (--publish only): chore(release): X and vX. 4. The updater. The committed tauri.conf.json carries the placeholder ${LUMEN UPDATER PUBKEY}. The release fills in the public key and the endpoint on GitHub Releases (stable: releases/latest/download/latest.json; a beta: the rolling beta-channel release). It also turns on signed update bundles. The build stops if the key is empty, is still the placeholder or is not a minisign key. Afterwards the file goes back to the placeholder. 5. A reproducible web build. repro-check builds twice with SOURCE DATE EPOCH and compares every file, then the bundle budget and the source-map check run. lumen-web-vX.tgz is the same bytes on every machine: the files are sorted, the owner and mode are fixed, and the gzip header has no time. 6. Desktop. tauri build runs with TAURI SIGNING PRIVATE KEY. The macOS update bundle gets its version and architecture in its name. latest.json is built from the .sig files. Every signature is checked against the updater key, and the same check must refuse a copy with one byte changed. 7. SBOM. sbom.cdx.json (CycloneDX 1.5) lists every package in package-lock.json and every crate in Cargo.lock. It is built offline. 8. Release notes. Hebrew first, then English, from release-notes/ .he.md and release-notes/ .en.md (written by hand, a few lines each), then the full change list and how to verify the download. 9. Checksums. SHA256SUMS lists every asset. It is signed with minisign (SHA256SUMS.minisig), and so is the SBOM. The whole folder is then verified, and a changed SHA256SUMS must fail. 10. Publish (--publish only): git push origin HEAD vX, then gh release create. A beta is a pre-release and is never "latest", so stable users never get it. Then latest.json is uploaded to the beta-channel release.

pages.md:
Every Lumen deployment serves an open roadmap at `/roadmap.html` (and at
`/roadmap` on Cloudflare Pages, Netlify and the Docker image). The status bar's
**Roadmap** link opens it.

## Where it comes from

The page is the third output of `npm run plan`, next to the board in
`MASTER_PLAN.md` and `plan/board.html`. All three are rendered from one file,
`plan/plan.json`, and `npm run plan:check` fails CI when any of them differs
from it. So the roadmap changes in the same commit as the plan, every time.

## What it shows — and what it does not

| Shown | Not shown |
|---|---|
| every phase, with its number and title | the steps of a task and its acceptance line |
| every task's number and title | estimates, dates and the schedule |
| its state: **done** (✅), **in progress** (⏳) or **planned** | branches, PR numbers and the owner's items (phase 15) |
| the counts and a progress bar | anything from issues or notes |

The full plan, with every measured acceptance criterion, is in the repository.

## How it renders

`public/roadmap.html` carries the data as a JSON block; `public/roadmap.js`
builds the cards with `textContent`. The script is external because the app's
Content-Security-Policy allows no inline script, and it needs no Trusted Types
policy because it never writes HTML. The page is Hebrew and right-to-left,
laid out with logical CSS properties.

## Updating it

```bash
npm run plan        # rewrites MASTER_PLAN.md's board, plan/board.html and public/roadmap.html
npm run plan:check  # what CI runs: exit 1 when any of them is out of date
```

pages.title: Sustainability
pages.description: How Lumen pays for itself without ads, accounts or locked features. Donations through GitHub Sponsors and Open Collective, an optional paid relay that sees only ciphertext, and every cost in the open.
pages.md:
Lumen is open source and mostly built by one person. This page is the plan for keeping it running. The live, script-free summary is the [support page](https://lumen-md.vercel.app/support.html).

## Principles

- **Every feature stays free and local.** Nothing in the app is locked behind a payment.
- **Money pays for hosting only.** The one paid product is an optional managed sync relay. Running your own relay stays free (`node sync-server/vault-relay.js`, from sync in two clicks, #483).
- **The paid relay sees no content,** the same as the free one. Notes are encrypted on the device before they leave it ([encrypted sync](/sync/e2ee/)).
- **Every cost is public.** The support page lists what Lumen pays each month, and `scripts/cost-model.mjs` computes the paid tier's numbers. A test checks that the page and the model agree.

## What it costs today

| Service | What for | Per month |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Vercel Hobby | The app at lumen-md.vercel.app | $0 |
| Cloudflare Workers, free plan | The [public live-share server](/collab/public-server/) | $0 |
| GitHub | Code, issues, releases | $0 |

**Total: $0.** Vercel's Hobby plan is for non-commercial use only. Asking for donations is allowed, but selling anything, the relay included, is commercial use under [Vercel's fair-use guidelines](https://vercel.com/docs/limits/fair-use-guidelines). Before the paid relay launches, the app moves to a host that allows commercial use, or to Vercel Pro (plan W4.27).

## Donations

| Channel | Fee | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [GitHub Sponsors](https://docs.github.com/en/sponsors/getting-started-with-github-sponsors/about-github-sponsors), personal account | 0% from personal sponsors. Organizations pay up to 6% (3% card processing and 3% service). | No fee, and Israel is a supported region for receiving money. |
| [Open Collective](https://opencollective.com) through [Open Source Collective](https://opencollective.com/opensource/apply/intro) | 10% host fee, plus the card processor's fee | A public ledger: every donation and every expense, with receipts. |

### Choosing a fiscal host (researched 12.11.2026)

A fiscal host holds the money, keeps the books and pays expenses for a collective that has no legal entity of its own.

| Host | Fit for Lumen | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Open Source Collective** | **Chosen** | Hosts open-source projects. Host fee 10% ([application page](https://opencollective.com/opensource/apply/intro)). Verification through GitHub, or manual review. |
| Open Collective Europe | No | For projects rooted in or connected to Europe ([Open Collective's list of hosting options](https://blog.opencollective.com/fiscal-hosting-options)). |
| Open Collective Foundation | No | Dissolved on 31.12.2024 ([announcement](https://blog.opencollective.com/open-collective-official-statement-ocf-dissolution/)). |
| Huddlecraft | No | UK-based projects or projects in GBP. 4.25% plus a £50 setup fee. |
| The Social Change Nest | Possible | A UK CIC that can host groups outside the UK. It hosts social causes, not specifically software. |

Payouts from Open Source Collective reach an Israeli bank account through Wise or PayPal. Their fees depend on the currency and the country ([payment processor fees](https://documentation.opencollective.com/expenses-and-getting-paid/payment-processor-fees)).

## The paid relay (optional, planned)

### What it is

The same blob protocol as the relay of sync in two clicks (`sync-server/vault-relay.js`, #483), run by Lumen for people who don't want to run their own. The app talks to it exactly as it talks to a self-hosted relay. The only difference is `VITE_SYNC_RELAY_URL`. There are no accounts in the app.

### Where it runs

On the Cloudflare account that already runs the public live-share server (#469, `edge-workers/collab/`), as a second Worker:

- **R2** holds the objects. Each key is the SHA-256 of the space plus the object name, which is already an HMAC chosen by the app.
- **One Durable Object per space** makes `If-Match` / `If-None-Match` writes atomic and keeps the object list, the ETags and the byte count in its SQLite storage. The relay's store interface (`createVaultRelay({ store })`) is the seam: an R2 store plus a per-space Durable Object lock implement the same `list / get / put / delete / bytes / sweep` methods that the tests already check.
- Limits: 10 GB per paid space, 25 MiB per object, and the same rate limit as the Node relay. Request logging stays off, as for #469.

### What it sees

| | The paid relay |
| --- | --- |
| Note text, titles, file names | **Never.** The device encrypts everything, and object names are HMACs. |
| Your key or recovery words | **Never.** The space is named by a token derived from the words (#483). The relay keeps only the token's SHA-256. |
| Sizes and times of encrypted objects | Yes |
| Who paid | No. That stays with the payment provider. The relay keeps only a keyed hash of the licence, tied to one space (see below). |

### Paying without an account

1. Phase 1: a **licence key** from the merchant of record (Polar issues licence keys with each purchase). The app sends it once, together with the space token. The Worker checks it against the provider's API and stores `HMAC(secret, licence id) → (space hash, plan, expiry)`. The provider knows who paid but never learns the space. The relay knows the space but not who paid. The two can be linked only by combining both records.
2. Phase 2: **unlinkable tokens**, with blind signatures (RSA blind signatures, RFC 9474, as used in Privacy Pass). The payment issues blinded tokens and the relay redeems them, so not even the combined records connect a payer to a space.
3. When a subscription ends, the space becomes read-only for 30 days and is deleted after 90 days. Every device still has the notes. Free self-hosting stays one command away.

## Cost per user and break-even

From `node scripts/cost-model.mjs`, with list prices checked on 12.11.2026: [Workers](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/pricing/), [Durable Objects](https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/platform/pricing/), [R2](https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/pricing/) and [Polar](https://polar.sh/docs/fees). The usage assumption is an active note-taker with 2–3 devices: 1 GB encrypted, about 100 writes and 1,000 reads a day.

| Per paying user per month | USD |
| --- | --- |
| R2 storage (1 GB) | $0.0150 |
| R2 writes (3,000) | $0.0135 |
| R2 reads (30,000) | $0.0108 |
| Worker requests | $0.0099 |
| Durable Object requests | $0.0005 |
| **Infrastructure total** | **$0.0496** |

| | Monthly plan, $3 | Yearly plan, $30 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Payment fee per payment (Polar Starter, 5% + $0.50, +1.5% for a non-US card) | $0.6950 | $2.45 |
| Left per subscriber per month | $2.26 | $2.25 |

| Fixed per month | USD | Break-even |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Workers Paid ($5) + a domain (about $10.44 a year), app on a free host | $5.87 | **3 subscribers** |
| The same, app on Vercel Pro ($20) | $25.87 | **12 subscribers** |

The model does not count the owner's time or an accountant's fee. Those depend on the owner's choices (see below). Storage dominates only for very large vaults: at the 10 GB cap, a user costs about $0.18 a month.

## Taking payments

| Option | For an Israeli seller | Verdict |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Polar** (merchant of record) | Pays out to Israel through Stripe Connect Express ([supported countries](https://polar.sh/docs/merchant-of-record/supported-countries)). Starter: 5% + $0.50, +1.5% for cards outside the US. Licence keys built in. Its code is open source. | **Chosen** |
| Paddle (merchant of record) | 5% + $0.50. Mature, aimed at software companies, with a review before selling. | Fallback |
| Lemon Squeezy (merchant of record) | 5% + $0.50. Now owned by Stripe and moving to Stripe Managed Payments, which supports merchants in 35+ countries ([2026 update](https://www.lemonsqueezy.com/blog/2026-update)). Israel is not confirmed. | Not now |
| Stripe directly | Israel is not on [Stripe's list of supported countries](https://stripe.com/global). It would need a US company (Stripe Atlas), and Lumen would have to collect and remit VAT and sales tax worldwide itself. | Rejected |

A merchant of record is the legal seller to each subscriber. It charges and remits the subscriber's VAT or sales tax in the subscriber's country, handles refunds and chargebacks, and pays the developer. With one, Lumen sells to one foreign company instead of to people in many tax systems.

### Israeli VAT and income tax (for the owner and an accountant)

- **Osek patur (exempt dealer).** No VAT is charged. Turnover must stay under the yearly ceiling: ₪122,833 in 2026, counting all of the business's turnover. This is the simplest start.
- **Osek murshe (licensed dealer).** A service given to a foreign resident, such as the merchant of record, can be zero-rated under section 30(a)(5) of the VAT Law. The section excludes a service that is in practice also given to an Israeli resident in Israel. The VAT Authority could read Israeli subscribers as that case and expect 18% on their share. Get a ruling, or report 18% on the payouts for Israeli customers. The provider's reports show each customer's country.
- **Donations** through Open Source Collective are paid out against expenses or invoices. Payouts from GitHub Sponsors are income too. GitHub asks a non-US recipient for a W-8BEN.
- This is a plan, not tax advice. An Israeli accountant (רואה חשבון) confirms it before the first sale.

## Owner steps

1. **GitHub Sponsors.** Enroll the personal account at github.com/sponsors: payout profile, W-8BEN, and tiers (for example $3, $10, $25). Then uncomment `github:` in `.github/FUNDING.yml`.
2. **Open Collective.** Create the collective `lumen-md` and apply to Open Source Collective (verify through GitHub). Once it is accepted, uncomment `open_collective:` in `.github/FUNDING.yml`.
3. **Accountant.** Choose between osek patur and osek murshe, get the section 30(a)(5) question answered for a merchant of record, and set up bookkeeping.
4. **Hosting (W4.27).** Before the first sale, move the app off Vercel Hobby, to a host that allows commercial use or to Vercel Pro.
5. **Polar.** Create the organisation and one product, "Lumen sync relay", at $3 a month or $30 a year, with licence keys. Connect the payout account (Stripe Connect Express, Israel). The Polar API token becomes a Worker secret.
6. **Cloudflare.** Turn on Workers Paid ($5), create the R2 bucket, and deploy the vault relay Worker (a follow-up to this plan; the code seam is described above).
7. **Privacy policy and terms.** Update the privacy policy (#456) for what the provider and the relay keep, and add short terms for the paid relay.
8. **Every month.** Update the support page's cost table and the cost model's prices from the real invoices, and post the same numbers on Open Collective.

pages.title: Usability tests with Hebrew speakers
pages.description: How Lumen is tested with people who write in Hebrew — the ten tasks, SUS, the consent-first session recorder that keeps no note text, and the analysis.
pages.md:
The project measures a lot, and sessions with real people measure what
nothing else does: whether someone who writes in Hebrew can do the common
things without help. The kit is in
[`research/usability/`](https://github.com/talstilkol/lumen-md/tree/main/research/usability)
and everything in it is in Hebrew, the participants' language.

## The study

- **Who:** 8 participants per round, at least 5: two students, two
  researchers, two writers and two developers. All work in Hebrew and are new
  to Lumen.
- **What:** ten tasks, one at a time, thinking aloud, with no help from the
  moderator:
  1. a new note;
  2. a checklist;
  3. linking notes;
  4. search;
  5. tags;
  6. Hebrew and English on one line;
  7. a table;
  8. export to PDF;
  9. restoring from the trash;
  10. the daily note.
- **Measured:**
  - success, success without help, and time, per task;
  - the ease question (SEQ, 1–7) after each task;
  - the System Usability Scale (SUS, 0–100) at the end.
- **Rounds:** the ten most severe issues from round 1 become plan tasks.
  Round 2, with new participants, checks the fixes. The goal is a mean SUS
  of at least 80, at least 90% unaided success, and all ten severe issues
  closed. The study is repeated before every major release.

## Take the test on your own

You can help without a meeting. The session takes about 30 minutes, on your own.

1. Open lumen-md.vercel.app in a **private window**.
2. Open the command palette (Ctrl+K, or ⌘K on a Mac) and choose **Usability test (self-guided)…**.
3. Read what is recorded and agree.

What happens then:

- Lumen gives you a random code such as `U-7K3F`, never your name.
- It adds a few practice notes to a folder named `בדיקת שימושיות`.
- It shows ten short tasks one at a time. You press **Done** or **I couldn't do it**, then rate how easy the task was.
- At the end come ten short statements about Lumen.

Where a task's result can be seen in the practice notes, Lumen checks it on
your device and keeps only **yes or no**, never the text.

At the end you save one `.zip` file and send it through the link in your
invitation. Then press **Delete my session data**. Nothing is sent until you
send the file yourself.

## The session recorder

Command palette → **Usability study (moderator)…** opens the moderator's
panel. It is off until then, and it records nothing until the participant
has signed the consent form and the moderator ticks the box.

| Recorded | Never recorded |
|---|---|
| when each task started and ended, and its outcome | anything typed into notes, note or file names |
| controls clicked, by role and by the app's own label | a label that isn't one of the app's UI strings (it becomes `[label]`) |
| commands run, by id | the participant's name (a code: P1, P2, …) |
| how many keys were pressed, and modifier shortcuts | which characters were typed |
| the SEQ and SUS answers, and the moderator's observation codes | free-text notes (the moderator keeps those on paper) |

- **Local:** the data stays in the browser and leaves only as the JSON file
  the moderator saves. The recorder makes no request.
- **Deletion:** *Delete session data* removes it, and anything left on the
  device is deleted after 30 days. The consent form promises that session
  files are deleted once the round's analysis is written.

## The analysis

`node scripts/usability-analyze.mjs <folder> --round 1` turns a round's
session files into a report:

- per task: success, success without help, median time, SEQ, errors and
  help opened;
- SUS per participant, and the mean with a 95% confidence interval.

With `--round 2 --findings …` it also checks the plan's acceptance criteria
against the findings file. With 5–8 people the numbers show a direction,
not statistical significance.

The Hebrew SUS wording is the study's own translation, not a validated one.
It compares rounds with each other; comparisons with published SUS norms
are approximate.

pages.title: Data-safety drill
pages.description: Every way Lumen saves a note to a folder, driven through kill -9, a full disk, lost permissions and another program editing at the same time, with a report per release.
pages.md:
The drill checks the claim that a note is never half-saved. It drives
**each way Lumen writes a note to a folder** through four kinds of trouble,
on a real disk with real processes:

| Trouble | What happens |
|---|---|
| **kill -9** | A process saves notes as fast as it can and is killed with `SIGKILL` at a random moment, 1,000 times |
| **Full disk** | A note grows until a save no longer fits on a small file system (`ENOSPC`) |
| **Lost permission** | The folder and its notes become read-only in the middle of saving |
| **Another program** | An editor or a sync client saves the same notes (temporary file, then rename) while Lumen saves |

Each saved version carries a SHA-256 of its own text. After every round each
note must be **one whole version**, no older than before, and still there.
A save that fails must fail loudly, so the app keeps the text and tries
again.

The save paths it drives are the phone folder (`src/storage/vault/mobile.ts`,
the real code), the OPFS worker that Safari before 26 uses, the desktop app's
write in `src-tauri/vault/src/lib.rs` (its algorithm; `cargo test` checks the
Rust itself), and the atomic save of plan W1.5 when the checkout has it. The
browser's File System Access path is atomic by design and is covered by the
e2e matrix (`e2e/data-safety.spec.ts`).

## Run it

```sh
npm run drill:data-safety -- --kills 1000 --full-disk /mnt/small
```

`--full-disk` takes a small file system you mounted for the test (on Linux:
`sudo mount -t tmpfs -o size=256k tmpfs /mnt/small`); without it the full-disk
part is skipped. Run as root, the saving process drops to an unprivileged
user so the permission test means something.

The report goes to `reports/data-safety-drill-<commit>.md` and `.json`, one
per release. The exit code is 0 only when no note was damaged or lost.

pages.title: Allowed image hosts
pages.description: See which sites may always load images in your notes, and revoke one or all of them.
pages.md:
An image from another site tells that site you opened the note. So Lumen
doesn't load it until you say so: the preview shows a placeholder with
**Load** (this image, until you reload the page) and **Always allow**
(every image from that site, in this browser).

## The list, and revoking

Command palette → **Privacy: allowed image hosts…** lists every site you
chose **Always allow** for.

- **Revoke** next to a site: its images wait for you again, at once — the
  preview shows the placeholder and nothing more is requested from that
  site. Images from it you loaded once with **Load** in this session are
  blocked again too.
- **Revoke all** does it for every site.

The list is kept in this browser (localStorage), not in your notes or your
vault, so another browser or device has its own.

The desktop app loads no images from other sites at all; there is nothing
to allow there.

pages.title: Journalist mode: redaction and locked notes
pages.description: Text you redact is removed from every export, not covered. A note can be locked with a password of its own.
pages.md:
Reporters, lawyers and researchers keep notes about people who must not be
named. Lumen has two tools for that, on top of [photo metadata
removal](/security/photo-metadata/).

## True redaction

Select the text and run **Redact selection** from the command palette. The
text is wrapped in `<redact>…</redact>`: you still see it in your note,
shaded, and it is **removed** from every export — PDF, print, DOCX, HTML,
Markdown, RTF, LaTeX, EPUB, slides and the rest. In its place the export has
`█████`, always five blocks, so the length of a name gives nothing away.

This is not a black box drawn over text that is still there (a well-known
leak in PDFs: copy the box, or run `pdftotext`, and the text comes back).
The exporters never receive the text at all.

The rules fail closed:

- A `<redact>` that is never closed removes everything after it, and every
  footnote too: the preview shows the footnotes at the end of the note, so they
  are shaded with the rest.
- A mark with attributes or a slash (`<redact class="x">`, `<redact/>`) is a
  mark too, exactly as the preview reads it, so what you see shaded is what
  goes.
- **Redact selection** over text that already has marks makes one mark over
  the whole selection; nothing that was covered before is uncovered.
- Photos inlined as `data:` URLs are judged by their bytes, whatever their
  label, and so are photos embedded in an SVG: a JPEG, PNG or WebP loses its
  metadata, and one that can't be cleaned (HEIC, AVIF) is left out.
- Marks count inside code blocks too.
- A `</redact>` that the preview doesn't read as one (in code, in a link's
  address, in a comment, or while a paragraph or table opened inside the
  passage is still open) doesn't end the passage. Everything the preview
  shades is gone from the export, and sometimes a little more. A suggestion
  (`{>>comment<<}`, `{~~old~>new~~}`) is read the way the preview reads it,
  so its `>` doesn't end a tag that the preview keeps open.
- The same goes for Markdown structure. A `<redact>` on a line of its own
  shades the blocks after it, and a `</redact>` typed inside one of them (a
  list item, a quote, a table cell, a heading or a paragraph) doesn't end the
  passage. To end it, put the `</redact>` on a line of its own, after a blank
  line:

  ```markdown
  <redact>

  - Source A
  - Source B

  </redact>
  ```
- Exports also leave out hidden text a reader of the file could find: HTML
  comments (`<!-- … -->`) and Obsidian comments (`%% … %%`).
- **Print** (⌘P) of a note with redactions goes through the same export.
- **Publish site** (GitHub Pages or a .zip) and the command line (`lumen publish`,
  `lumen convert`) go through it too: the pages, their titles and the site's search
  index never hold a redacted passage, and the photos they copy lose their metadata.

What it does not do: the note itself keeps the text (that is the point), so
syncing or sharing the *note* shares the text. Redact before you export, and
share the export.

## A note with its own password

Run **Note password…** on a note saved in the vault. The note is encrypted
with a password of its own, separate from the vault's: on disk, in sync and
in backups it is ciphertext, with one line saying how to open it.

- **Opening:** open the note, run **Note password…**, type the password. It
  stays open until you choose **Lock now** or close Lumen; the password is
  never stored.
- **While it is open,** what Lumen keeps on the device (the open tabs, the
  version history) keeps the encrypted text, not the plain one. Locking a
  note deletes its earlier, plain versions from history.
- **Forgotten password = lost note.** There is no recovery key, by design.
- **While it is locked,** nothing replaces the note but its own encrypted
  text, byte for byte: plain text from a tool or an old tab is refused, and
  so is any other encrypted text, even one that copies the note's salt.
- The key comes from the password through the vault's key-derivation
  function (PBKDF2-SHA256, 600,000 iterations today; Argon2id once it lands),
  and every save is sealed with AES-256-GCM under a fresh nonce.

Limits, plainly: the note's *name* is not hidden; "Save as" makes a plain
copy; anything you copy out of an open note is plain text; and a device
that is compromised while the note is open can read it.

pages.title: Monitoring and web vitals
pages.description: Error reports are off by default and sent only with your consent; web vitals never leave your device.
pages.md:
Lumen measures how fast it is on your device, and can send crash reports
to an error tracker, but only after you turn them on. Both work the same
way in every build.

## Web vitals: measured here, never sent

Lumen measures five page-speed metrics with the browser's
`PerformanceObserver`:

| Metric | What it is | Good |
|---|---|---|
| LCP | Largest Contentful Paint: when the largest visible element appears | ≤ 2.5 s |
| FCP | First Contentful Paint: when the first content appears | ≤ 1.8 s |
| TTFB | Time to First Byte: when the server's first response byte arrives | ≤ 800 ms |
| INP | Interaction to Next Paint: the slowest interaction this session | ≤ 200 ms |
| CLS | Cumulative Layout Shift: how much the layout jumps without your input | ≤ 0.1 |

The values stay in memory on your device. Open them with **Runtime
metrics** in the status bar, or from the command palette. They are never
sent, even when error reports are on. A sample stores no page address.

## Error reports: off by default

Lumen sends error reports only when **both** of these are true:

1. **You turned them on.** Click the **Telemetry** pill in the status bar.
   It is off in a fresh install. Click it again to turn reports off.
   Turning them off takes effect at once, even for an error that is
   already being reported.
2. **The build names an error tracker** in `VITE_SENTRY_DSN`. This can be
   Sentry or a self-hosted GlitchTip, which speaks the same protocol.

If either one is missing, the Sentry SDK is never downloaded and no
request is made. The default build has no DSN, so it makes no monitoring
requests at all. An e2e test (`e2e/monitoring.spec.ts`) checks this.

### What a report contains

Each report is rebuilt from a short allowlist before it leaves the browser:

- the error's class name, such as `TypeError`;
- the script file names, functions and line numbers of the stack trace;
- the app's release and environment, and the SDK's name and version.

The error **message is never sent**. A message can contain a title or a
line of a note without quotes ("Failed to save Quarterly plan"), and no
filter can reliably tell that apart from the app's own words. The stack
trace shows where the error happened, and that is enough to find it.

A report never includes:

- the error message, or any text logged with it;
- the page address;
- breadcrumbs, such as clicks, console lines and requests;
- user or IP data (`infer_ip: never`);
- tags, extra data or contexts.

There is no session replay, no performance tracing and no session
tracking.

### Every report is in the privacy ledger

Error reports go through the privacy ledger (command palette → **Privacy
ledger**) like every other request that leaves the device. Each one is listed under its own
category: "Error report — only with your consent, content removed". The
ledger shows where the report went, its size and its status. Under the
**local-only** AI policy, reports are refused before they leave, and each
refusal is listed as blocked.

## For operators: setting the DSN

Set the DSN at build time:

```bash
VITE_SENTRY_DSN=https://<public-key>@o123.ingest.sentry.io/4567 npm run build
# Docker: docker build --build-arg VITE_SENTRY_DSN=… .
```

**A DSN is not a secret.** Sentry designs it to be public: it ships in
every page that uses Sentry, and it only lets a client *submit* events
to one project. It can't read data. So a build-time `VITE_*` variable is
the right place for it, and secret scanners may ignore it.

The DSN's host is added to the CSP `connect-src` **automatically at build
time**, through the same mechanism as the other deployment endpoints
(`src/build/cspEndpoints.ts`). That covers the `index.html` meta tag,
`dist/_headers` and the nginx image. On **Vercel**, `vercel.ts` adds the
same origin to the header it serves, from the project's `VITE_SENTRY_DSN`
environment variable. No error-tracker host or wildcard is in the
checked-in policies.

Under the local-only AI policy, reports are refused before they leave, and each refusal is listed as blocked.

sections.heading: For operators: setting the DSN
sections.text: Set the DSN at build time: A DSN is not a secret. Sentry designs it to be public: it ships in every page that uses Sentry, and it only lets a client submit events to one project. It can't read data. So a build-time VITE variable is the right place for it, and secret scanners may ignore it. The DSN's host is added to the CSP connect-src automatically at build time , through the same mechanism as the other deployment endpoints (src/build/cspEndpoints.ts). That covers the index.html meta tag, dist/ headers and the nginx image. On Vercel , vercel.ts adds the same origin to the header it serves, from the project's VITE SENTRY DSN environment variable. No error-tracker host or wildcard is in the checked-in policies.

pages.description: How Lumen checks that the tests of its security-critical code, such as encryption, the keyring, sync merges and the privacy ledger, really catch bugs.
pages.md:
Coverage tells you which lines ran, not whether a test would notice if they
were wrong. Mutation testing checks that. It plants small bugs in the code,
one at a time, and runs the tests each time. A test suite that still passes
with a bug in place has missed it.

## What is tested

The pure modules whose bugs would hurt most:

- **Encryption primitives:** ChaCha20-Poly1305, BLAKE2b, scrypt and Argon2id.
- **age** file encryption, and the **keyring** that holds the vault keys and
  devices.
- The **sync engine**: conflict merging, the manifest and blob headers.
- The **privacy ledger**, which records and blocks anything that would leave
  the device.
- The **secret store** (API keys and tokens: encrypted in the browser, or in
  the OS keychain on desktop), the **raw-HTML sanitizer** of the preview,
  Hebrew **text matching**, file **encryption**, **ZIP** import limits, and
  the **agent runtime**.

The list is in `scripts/mutation/targets.json`.

## The bugs it plants

| Kind | Example |
|---|---|
| Operators | `+` ↔ `-`, `<` ↔ `<=`, `===` ↔ `!==`, `&&` ↔ `\|\|`, `<<` ↔ `>>`, `^` → `&` |
| Constants | `n` → `n + 1` (`1` → `0`) |
| Booleans | `true` ↔ `false` |
| Negation | `!x` → `x` |
| Conditions | `if (c)` → `if (!(c))` |

Only code is mutated, never types, imports or comments. A mutant that
doesn't parse is left out. A mutant counts as **caught** when a test that
passes on the real code fails, when the run crashes, or when it hangs.

## Running it

```sh
npm run test:mutation                          # all modules, fails under 70%
node scripts/mutation/run.mjs --module keyring # one module
node scripts/mutation/run.mjs --max 200        # a bigger sample per module
```

The report, with the score per module and every surviving mutant's line, is
written to `reports/mutation/`. The plan's target is a score of at least
70% per module. A mutant that survives in a security module should get a
test that catches it.

- the privacy ledger

- scores under 80%, or

pages.title: Photo metadata
pages.description: Photos you paste or drop into a note lose their GPS position, time, device and text metadata before they are stored.
pages.md:
A photo from a phone or a camera usually says **where** it was taken (GPS),
**when**, on **which device** (make, model, sometimes a serial number) and
sometimes **who** took it. If you share the note, export it or sync it,
that information goes with the photo.

Lumen removes it the moment you paste or drop a JPEG, PNG or WebP into a
note, before the image is stored in the vault or put inline:

- **Removed:** EXIF (GPS, date and time, camera, owner), XMP, IPTC,
  comments, PNG text and time chunks, Content Credentials (C2PA), and
  anything else the image doesn't need to be drawn. Only a fixed list of
  parts that draw the image is kept.
- **Kept:** the pixels, exactly as they were (nothing is re-compressed), the
  colour profile, and the photo's orientation, so a portrait photo still
  stands upright.

Lumen decides what a photo is from its contents, not from its name or the
type the browser reports. A JPEG named `.jfif` is cleaned like any JPEG.
A HEIC or AVIF photo (an iPhone original, even one named `.jpg`), and a
TIFF, can't be cleaned in place. Lumen redraws it through the canvas when
the browser can read it. Otherwise the photo is not added. GIF and SVG
images are stored as they are.

**When a photo can't be read:** the cleaning fails closed. A JPEG, PNG or WebP
whose structure Lumen can't parse is re-drawn through the browser's canvas,
which keeps only the pixels. If that isn't possible either, the photo is not
added (you see a message), and an export or a published site leaves it out.
Anything stored after the image's end is removed too: a second image (MPF,
used by some phones for depth or a preview) or the video of a motion photo.

**On export too:** photos already in the vault (including ones added before
this cleaning existed) are inlined clean into PDF and HTML exports, and
photos inlined in the note as `data:` URLs are cleaned in every export.
Publish site and `lumen publish` copy photos clean, whatever their file
names. They leave out HEIC, AVIF and TIFF photos and videos, whose metadata
(a video's location, for example) they can't remove, and list them as not
published. The file in the vault itself is not changed.

To keep the metadata (for example, for your own photo archive): **Settings →
General →** "Keep photos' location, time and camera details". Importing a
settings file never turns this switch on by itself.

pages.title: A privacy report you can prove
pages.description: Export the privacy ledger as a signed report, check it with a script, and see the results of the outside audit for every version.
pages.md:
"Private" is a claim. Lumen lets you check it. The privacy ledger lists
every network request Lumen's features make. You can export it as a
**signed report**, check that report with a script, and compare it with
what an **outside network analyzer** saw during the same run.

## Export the report

⌘K → *Privacy ledger…* → **Export signed report**. The file covers this
session, from when the tab opened. For each request it says:

| | |
|---|---|
| Who | Which feature (its category and reason: "Anthropic (Claude)", "Model download", …) |
| When | The time |
| Where | The host |
| How much | Bytes sent and received, and whether it was allowed or blocked |

The summary (requests, how many left the device and to which hosts, bytes)
is computed from those entries. The file holds no prompt, note or header.

It is signed in the browser with **Ed25519**, using a key made on this device
the first time you export. The private half stays in IndexedDB and can't be
exported. The signature uses the minisign format, so both the script below
and the `minisign` tool can verify it.

## Check a report

```sh
node scripts/privacy/verify-report.mjs lumen-privacy-report-….json
node scripts/privacy/verify-report.mjs report.json --local-only          # also: nothing left the device
node scripts/privacy/verify-report.mjs report.json --pub device.pub      # pin the signing key
node scripts/privacy/verify-report.mjs report.json --extract out/        # then: minisign -Vm out/report.json -p out/report.pub
```

The script checks the signature and the trusted comment (which names the
report's SHA-256), and that the report is in its canonical form. It checks
the shape of every entry: times inside the session and in order,
`leftDevice` following the ledger's rule. It then **works the summary out
again** and refuses a report whose summary disagrees with its entries.
Without `--pub`, it proves the file hasn't changed since it was signed. With
`--pub`, it also proves which device signed it.

## Audit mode

The ledger normally lists AI traffic. In **audit mode**
(`localStorage["lumen.privacy.audit"] = "1"`) it also lists every other
request that leaves the device and the LAN, as *Other request*. Those are
listed but never blocked. The app is then run through an outside analyzer:

```sh
node scripts/privacy/audit.mjs --sign ~/.lumen-release/lumen-release.key --publish
```

1. **mitmproxy** (`mitmdump`, 10.1 or newer) records every request,
   including the app's own requests to the dev server, which proves it was
   in the path.
2. `e2e/privacy-audit.spec.ts` runs the journey under the **local-only**
   policy with cloud keys set to tempt every fallback: the views, an export,
   the AI commands, and a hand-made cloud request (which is blocked). It then
   exports the signed report and keeps Playwright's own request log.
3. The script verifies the report and compares it with **both** observers.
   The audit passes only when each observer saw traffic, nothing it saw
   leaving is missing from the report, nothing the report lists is missing
   from the wire, and **0 requests are non-local**.
4. `audit.json` is signed with the [release key](/security/supply-chain/)
   and published below.

## Results per version

Every version since the first audit has its row. `publish.mjs --check`
fails when a released version (in `CHANGELOG.md`) has no audit file in
`security/privacy-audits/`.

<!-- audits:start -->
_No audit published yet: the first runs with the first release after this page._
<!-- audits:end -->

## Store privacy labels

`store/privacy-labels.json` is the source for the App Store's *App Privacy*
answers and Google Play's *Data safety* form:

- **Data not collected.** With default settings nothing leaves the device,
  which is what the local-only audit shows.
- **Crash data, only on one condition:** the build has a crash-reporting key
  and the user hasn't opted out. It isn't linked to the user and isn't used
  for tracking.
- Every optional feature that can send something, mapped to its category in
  the ledger.

A test keeps the labels in step with the ledger's categories, the crash
reporter and the published audits.

pages.title: Secret scan of the build
pages.description: Why no secret may be a VITE_* variable, the gate that fails a build that sets one, and the scan of the live deployments.
pages.md:
Vite copies the value of every `VITE_*` variable the app reads into the
public JavaScript. Anyone who opens the site can read it. So a token, an
API key or a password must never be a `VITE_*` variable. Lumen enforces
this in three places.

| Where | What it checks | What fails |
|---|---|---|
| The build (`vite build`) | Every `VITE_*` variable set in the environment or in an `.env` file | A name not on `security/vite-env-allowlist.json` |
| The Vercel preview gate (`npm run secrets:dist`) | Every file in `dist/` | A token shape, or an inlined `VITE_*` value not on the allowlist |
| The live scan (`npm run secrets:scan-live`) | Production, the 3 newest previews, and the `VITE_*` names set in Vercel | The same, plus a `VITE_*` name in Vercel that is not on the allowlist |

The code rules in `npm run hygiene` keep secret-named reads (`…TOKEN`,
`…SECRET`, `…KEY`) and reads of `import.meta.env` as a whole object out of
`src/`. Before #243 such a whole-object read put **every** `VITE_*`
variable of the build into the bundle, even ones the app never used. The
allowlist gate covers that case too: a build cannot set a name that is not
listed.

## The allowlist

`security/vite-env-allowlist.json` lists each name a build may set, with
the reason it is public: a worker URL, an OAuth client id, a price id, a
public key. Names that start with `VITE_VERCEL_` are Vercel's system
variables (the deployment id, the git branch and commit). They are not
secrets, and the app reads none of them. A value that starts with
`ci-canary-` is a test canary and is allowed under any name.

To add a variable, add its name and the reason it is public. If it is a
secret, it does not belong here: keep it in the secret store
(`src/lib/secretStore.ts`) or on the server.

## What the scan looks for

- **Secret** (the scan fails): OpenAI and Anthropic keys (`sk-`), GitHub
  tokens (`ghp_`, `github_pat_` …), Google API keys (`AIza`), AWS access
  keys, Stripe live keys, Slack tokens, private-key bodies, JWTs other
  than a public anon key, and inlined `VITE_*` values not on the allowlist.
- **For review** (listed only): hex strings of 32 or more characters, and
  anon JWTs. Content hashes and embed ids look the same.

A report never shows a whole value. It shows the first 4 characters and
the length.

## Running it

```bash
npm run secrets:self-test        # plants a token of each kind in a temporary build and finds it
npm run secrets:dist             # scans dist/ after npm run build
VERCEL_TOKEN=… VERCEL_PROJECT_ID=prj_… VERCEL_TEAM_ID=team_… \
  npm run secrets:scan-live -- --report scan.md
node scripts/secrets-scan-live.mjs --url https://lumen-md.vercel.app
```

The live scan reads the **names** of the project's environment variables
from the Vercel API. It never asks for a value to be decrypted. For a
protected preview, set `VERCEL_AUTOMATION_BYPASS_SECRET`.

## If a secret was a VITE_* variable (15.18)

1. Treat it as public. Any build that ran while it was set may have put it
   in the bundle, and old deployments stay online.
2. Revoke it with the provider and create a new one.
3. Delete the `VITE_*` variable in Vercel (and in Netlify or CI, if used).
4. Put the new value where it belongs: the secret store for a user's key,
   or a server-side secret for a worker.
5. Run `npm run secrets:scan-live` and keep the report.

If no secret was ever set as `VITE_*`, record that, and 15.18 is done.

For review (listed only): hex strings of 32 or more characters, and anon JWTs. Content hashes and embed ids look the same. A report never shows a whole value. It shows the first 4 characters and the length.

sections.heading: Running it
sections.text: The live scan reads the names of the project's environment variables from the Vercel API. It never asks for a value to be decrypted. For a protected preview, set VERCEL AUTOMATION BYPASS SECRET.

sections.heading: If a secret was a VITE variable (15.18)
sections.text: 1. Treat it as public. Any build that ran while it was set may have put it in the bundle, and old deployments stay online. 2. Revoke it with the provider and create a new one. 3. Delete the VITE variable in Vercel (and in Netlify or CI, if used). 4. Put the new value where it belongs: the secret store for a user's key, or a server-side secret for a worker. 5. Run npm run secrets:scan-live and keep the report. If no secret was ever set as VITE , record that, and 15.18 is done.

pages.md:
The [threat model](/security/threat-model/) assumes the code you run is the
code that was released. Four checks make that verifiable.

## 1. The decoders are fuzzed

Everything Lumen reads from a file, a link, the clipboard or a plugin goes
through a decoder: the Markdown pipeline, front matter, BibTeX, JSON and
JSONL (Code Doctor, Insights), URLs (sanitizer, embeds, the CSP check), text
direction — and `.base`, `.excalidraw`, PDF annotations and plugin
manifests as those land.

```bash
npm run fuzz                                    # 1,000,000 inputs per decoder
node scripts/fuzz/run.mjs --target bibtex --runs 50000
node scripts/fuzz/run.mjs --target bibtex --seed 1 --from 4242 --runs 1   # replay one input
```

Inputs are built from each format's own pieces (with Hebrew, Arabic, bidi
controls, emoji and lone surrogates), then cut, repeated and nested
thousands deep. Each decoder runs in its own worker: an exception it does
not document is a **crash**; one input running over a second is a **hang** —
the worker is stopped and the run continues. Failing inputs are saved to
`fuzz-findings/` with the command that replays them. The pass criterion is
0 crashes and 0 inputs over 1 s.

`--engine fast-check` runs the same decoders through
[fast-check](https://fast-check.dev) (with shrinking) once it is installed.

**Pathological Markdown (plan W4.16).** The first run found seven inputs
(8–14 KB) that took 0.5–2.8 s to render: thousands of `[` or `]` in one
paragraph, or lists nested 231 levels deep, make the parser's work grow with
the square of the text. A note like that would freeze the editor. Now a
block (the text between blank lines) with more than 256 brackets or more
than 32 nesting levels is shown as raw text, in a code block, exactly as
written (`src/renderer/boundMarkdown.ts`). Every real note stays far inside
both bounds and renders as before. The live preview also shows a block as
raw text once its render took more than 200 ms. The seven inputs are pinned
in `src/__tests__/markdownSlowInputs.test.ts` (each under 50 ms).

## 2. The build is reproducible

```bash
npm run repro
```

builds the same commit twice from clean (with `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` set to
the commit time) and compares the SHA-256 of every file in `dist/`. Any
difference is listed by file.

A release build has no source maps (plan 11.5), and the check fails if one
appears, so there is no map that could differ between two builds. Maps are
for a local investigation only (`LUMEN_SOURCEMAP=1`):
`node scripts/supply-chain/repro-check.mjs --sourcemap` builds with them and
says which fields of each differing map differ.

### On two machines and two infrastructures (plan W7.23)

A build that only reproduces on the machine that made it proves little. Two
more checks:

```bash
npm run repro:two-paths      # two clean checkouts of one commit, different everything
npm run repro:compare --  
```

- **`repro:two-paths`** builds the commit twice. The two builds differ in the
  checkout's absolute path (a long nested one with a space), every source
  file's modification time, `TZ`, `LANG`, `umask`, and the clock (under
  `faketime +400d` when it is installed). It then compares every file's SHA-256.
- **Cloudflare Workers Builds rebuilds every commit of `main`**
  (`scripts/supply-chain/cf-build.sh`, the Worker `cloudflare/repro/wrangler.jsonc`).
  It runs `npm ci` and `npm run build` from the same `package-lock.json`, and
  serves only the build's manifest at `<worker>/lumen-build.json`. The app
  stays on Vercel, whose `manifest` build gate writes the same manifest to
  `/.well-known/lumen-build.json`. The free plan gives 3,000 build minutes a month, one build at
  a time and 20 minutes per build (developers.cloudflare.com/workers/ci-cd/builds/limits-and-pricing).
- **The second host compares** (`scripts/supply-chain/repro-second-host.sh`). It
  hashes every file in the manifest as Vercel serves it for the same commit,
  appends the verdict to `reports/repro/ledger.jsonl`, and runs diffoscope on any
  file that differs. When the build is identical, it writes an in-toto statement
  ("built identically on two infrastructures") for the release attestation to sign.
- The target is 0 differing files, `.map` files included, on 10 commits in a row,
  with the Cloudflare build under 15 minutes.

## 3. Every release has an SBOM

```bash
npm run sbom          # → release/sbom.cdx.json
```

A CycloneDX 1.5 list of every npm package (`package-lock.json`) and every
Rust crate (`src-tauri/Cargo.lock`): version, package URL, the lockfile's
hash and the licence. Same lockfiles, same bytes.

## 4. Every release is signed — offline

The signing key belongs to the release owner and never enters a CI system.

**Once** (on the owner's machine):

```bash
LUMEN_RELEASE_PASSPHRASE=… node scripts/supply-chain/keys.mjs --out ~/.lumen-release
cp ~/.lumen-release/lumen-release.pub security/release-key.pub   # commit this file only
```

Keep `lumen-release.key` and its passphrase offline (a password manager
and a second offline copy). Old releases stay verifiable with the old
public key if the key is ever replaced.

**Each release:**

```bash
npm run repro && npm run build
LUMEN_RELEASE_PASSPHRASE=… npm run release:sign -- --key ~/.lumen-release/lumen-release.key \
  --artifact <each desktop / mobile file>
```

This writes `release/SHA256SUMS` (every file of `dist/` and each artifact),
`release/sbom.cdx.json` and a minisign signature of each, then checks the
result. Upload the four files with the release.

**Anyone can check a release:**

```bash
npm run release:verify                      # signatures + every file against SHA256SUMS
# or with the standard tools:
minisign -Vm SHA256SUMS -P <public key from security/release-key.pub>
sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS
```

The signatures are standard minisign (Ed25519 over BLAKE2b-512), made with
Node's own crypto — no extra package.

## OpenSSF Best Practices

The [OpenSSF Best Practices badge](https://www.bestpractices.dev) is
claimed by the project owner. What it asks for, and where it is:

| Criterion | Here |
|---|---|
| Public repo, licence, contribution and security-report docs | `LICENSE`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, `SECURITY.md` |
| Version-controlled, unique version per release, release notes | git tags, `CHANGELOG.md`, `RELEASE.md` |
| Automated tests and a test policy for new code | vitest + Playwright; every task's Definition of done |
| Static analysis and dependency scanning | ESLint, CodeQL, `npm audit`, `cargo audit`, gitleaks (`.github/workflows/security.yml`) |
| Dynamic analysis (fuzzing) | `npm run fuzz` |
| Signed releases, reproducible build | `npm run release:sign` / `release:verify`, `npm run repro` |
| A vulnerability report process with response times | `SECURITY.md` (acknowledged within 48 h, a fix timeline within 5 business days, 90-day disclosure) |

pages.title: The e2e test surface
pages.description: window.__lumen.agentReview exists only in development and tests.
pages.md:
The end-to-end tests drive a few app functions through `window.__lumen`.
One of them, `window.__lumen.agentReview`, stages a change for the
[agent review screen](/ai/agents/) the way an agent's write tool does. A
page script that could call it could put changes in front of you that no
agent proposed, so it is **not part of the app you install**.

## Where it exists

| Build | `window.__lumen.agentReview` |
|---|---|
| `npm run dev` (Vite dev server) | yes |
| `npx vitest` (unit tests) | yes |
| `VITE_LUMEN_TEST_SURFACE=1 npm run build` (the e2e-prod job only) | yes |
| `npm run build` (every release, the PWA, desktop and mobile) | **no** — the code is removed from the bundle |

The release build replaces `import.meta.env.DEV` and
`VITE_LUMEN_TEST_SURFACE` with constants, so the surface and the function
behind it are dropped when the bundle is minified.

## Checking a build

```sh
npm run build
npm run check:test-surface
```

`check:test-surface` reads every JavaScript file under `dist/` and fails if
one still sets or reads `.agentReview` (the translation keys such as
`agentReview.title` are text and do not count). CI runs it after the
production build.

pages.title: Threat model
pages.description: What Lumen protects, from whom, at each of its boundaries — vault, sync, sharing, plugins, agents and the web clipper — and where each defence is tested.
pages.md:
Privacy is Lumen's central claim, so it has to be checkable from the
outside. This page names, for every boundary where data crosses from one
party to another, the threats in each STRIDE category (**S**poofing,
**T**ampering, **R**epudiation, **I**nformation disclosure, **D**enial of
service, **E**levation of privilege), what stops them, and what is left.
Each defence points to the code or test that holds it; a row without one
is a known gap.

## What is protected

- **Notes and attachments** — the vault (browser storage, a folder, the
  phone).
- **Secrets** — AI keys, Git and cloud tokens, room passwords
  ([Secrets and encryption](/security/vault/)).
- **What the user types into AI** — prompts and the notes sent with them.
- **The app itself** — the code a user runs must be the code that was
  released ([Supply chain](/security/supply-chain/)).

## Who we defend against

| Attacker | Can | Cannot (assumed) |
|---|---|---|
| A malicious note or file (shared, imported, clipped, synced) | Put any bytes in a note, a `.canvas`, a front-matter block, a link | Run code outside the sandboxes |
| A network attacker / a relay or signaling server | Read and change traffic it carries | Break TLS or AES-GCM |
| A cloud provider (Dropbox, Drive, Gist) | Read, change, delete or hold back the files it stores | — |
| A plugin or live block | Run its own code in its sandbox | Reach the page's origin, the vault or the network without a granted capability |
| A cloud AI provider (only when the user chose one) | See what is sent to it | See anything under policy `local-only` |
| Someone with the device unlocked | Everything the user can | — (out of scope; OS lock and disk encryption) |
| A compromised dependency or build | Ship different code | Pass the signature and reproducible-build checks |

## Boundaries

### Vault (files on disk, browser storage, phone)

| | Threat | Defence | Where |
|---|---|---|---|
| T | A crash or kill half way through a save leaves a cut note | Atomic saves: temporary file, fsync, rename; recovery after restart | plan W1.5 (branch `feat/atomic-writes`, its crash test) |
| T | A path from a note, a zip or git leaves the vault (`../`) | Every path checked: no `.`/`..`/NUL segments; Rust checks the folder again | `src/storage/vault`, `src-tauri/vault` tests |
| I | A desktop WebView script reads other files | The WebView has no `fs:` permission; only the app's `vault_*` commands, inside the picked folder | `src-tauri/capabilities` |
| D | A huge or malformed file hangs the app | Decoders fuzzed: 1,000,000 inputs each, no crash, nothing over 1 s | `npm run fuzz` |
| R | "Who changed this note?" | Local history and git (when enabled); no server log exists to forge | history, safe git (3.3) |

### Sync (cloud providers, git)

| | Threat | Defence | Where |
|---|---|---|---|
| I | The provider reads the notes | End-to-end encryption before upload (plan 3.4/3.5); without it the provider sees plaintext — shown in the sync settings | `src/sync` |
| T | The provider changes or rolls back files | Authenticated encryption (AES-GCM) with versions (3.4); a conflict keeps both sides as `.conflict-<time>.md` | `src/sync/cloud/sync.ts` |
| D | The provider deletes everything | A deletion is never synced blindly; local trash and history | 3.7 data-safety matrix |
| S | A token leaks from storage | Tokens encrypted at rest; OS keychain on desktop | [Secrets](/security/vault/), `src/lib/secretStore.ts` |

### Sharing and live collaboration

| | Threat | Defence | Where |
|---|---|---|---|
| I | The signaling server or a relay reads the document | Yjs updates wrapped in AES-GCM, key from the room password (PBKDF2) | `src/collab/encryption.ts`, `e2e.ts` |
| S | Someone joins a room by knowing its name | The room password never leaves the device (it travels only in the link's `#` fragment); without it a peer gets ciphertext only | `src/collab/roomUrl.ts`, `encryption.ts` |
| T | A peer sends malformed updates | Bad tags are dropped; the document is rendered through the same sanitizer as any note | `src/collab/e2e.ts` |
| R | Edits cannot be attributed | Comments and version history carry the author locally; not a cryptographic proof (gap) | `src/collab/versionHistory.ts` |

### Plugins and live blocks

| | Threat | Defence | Where |
|---|---|---|---|
| E | Block code reaches the page, the vault or the keys | `sandbox="allow-scripts"` iframes without same-origin (an opaque origin); live-js runs only on click | `src/plugins/liveJsRunner.ts`; security e2e (plan 2.3) |
| I | A block exfiltrates over the network | CSP `connect-src` from one source; the sandbox has no network | `scripts/headers.mjs` (drift check) |
| T | Raw HTML in a note injects script | Allowlist sanitizer on raw HTML; Trusted Types | `src/renderer/rehypeSanitizeRaw.ts`, `src/lib/trustedTypes.ts` |
| E | A plugin asks for more than it says | Capabilities declared in the manifest, shown before install; scanner per version (plan 11.2, W1.20) | plugin registry |

### Agents and AI

| | Threat | Defence | Where |
|---|---|---|---|
| I | Prompts or notes reach a cloud model the user did not choose | AI policy, default `local-only`: a cloud provider is never contacted, not even as a fallback | `src/ai/policy.ts` |
| E | Prompt injection in a note makes an agent act | Every tool has a scope (`read` / `write` / `net`); a `write` or `net` tool runs only when that scope was granted for the run; workspace paths are checked | `src/agents/runtime.ts`, `src/agents/tools/workspace.ts` |
| T | A model's answer carries a link or HTML that runs | Answers render as Markdown through the sanitizer | renderer |
| D | A runaway request | Every request can be cancelled (AI: Cancel, Esc) | `src/ai/aiAbort.ts` |

### Web clipper (browser extension)

| | Threat | Defence | Where |
|---|---|---|---|
| E | The extension's broad host access is abused | It acts only on a user click (`activeTab`, context menu); no background reading of pages | `extension/manifest.json` |
| T | A clipped page carries script into a note | Clips become Markdown; raw HTML goes through the sanitizer | `extension/contentScript.js`, renderer |
| I | Clips leak to a server | The clip goes straight into the app; no Lumen server exists | — |

### Releases and dependencies

| | Threat | Defence | Where |
|---|---|---|---|
| T | A tampered download | `SHA256SUMS` + minisign signatures made offline; anyone checks with the public key | `npm run release:verify` |
| T | A build that differs from the source | Two clean builds must give the same SHA-256 per file | `npm run repro` |
| I/E | A malicious or vulnerable dependency | Lockfile only; npm audit, cargo audit, gitleaks (plan 2.8); an SBOM in every release | `.github/workflows/security.yml`, `scripts/audit-gate.mjs`, `sbom.cdx.json` |

## Known gaps

- Collaboration edits are attributed locally, not signed (R).
- An agent granted `write` writes without asking again for each file (E).
- A copied browser profile can use the stored secret key without a password
  until whole-vault encryption (11.4) ships.
- The clipper's `<all_urls>` host permission is broader than the
  click-only behaviour needs.
- The fuzzer covers the decoders on each branch; `.base`, `.excalidraw`,
  PDF annotations and plugin manifests join it as those modules land.

Found something? See [SECURITY.md](https://github.com/talstilkol/lumen-md/blob/main/SECURITY.md)
for private reporting.

pages.title: Trusted repositories
pages.description: Let agents propose changes in a git repository you own without the extra outside-content question.
pages.md:
Notes that come from a **git clone or pull** are *outside content*:
someone else may have written them, and they may hide instructions for
an agent (see [Local agents → Outside content](/ai/local-agents/#outside-content-prompt-injection)).
So when an agent has read such a note, every change it proposes asks you
first, before it is even staged.

For a repository that is yours, such as your own notes repo or a repo
only your team pushes to, that question gets in the way. **Trust this
repo** turns it off for that repository.

## Turn it on

1. Open the command palette (⌘K) and run **Trusted repositories…**
   (group *Security*).
2. Every repository cloned in this browser is listed with a switch. All
   of them start as **Asks first**.
3. Turn the switch on and confirm. The repository is now **Trusted**.

The setting is saved **on this device only**. It is not synced, not
written into the repository, and not shared with collaborators.

## What changes

With the switch on, when everything outside in an agent's run comes from
trusted repositories:

- a change the agent proposes is **staged without the extra question**;
- the change still **waits for your review** in the staged changes list.
  Nothing is written until you apply it.

## What stays the same

- The repository's notes are still **delimited and cleaned** in the
  prompt, and the run still records that it read outside content.
- **Web requests still ask** (fetch a page, search the web): that is how
  text planted in a note could send your data out.
- Anything else outside in the same run asks as before: a clipped page,
  an imported folder, a web result, another repository that is not
  trusted, or a note in the trusted repository whose frontmatter says
  `untrusted: true`.

## When trust is dropped

Trust belongs to the repository you looked at, so it is removed when:

- you **clone again** into the same folder;
- you **rename or move** the repository folder, or move another folder
  onto its name.

Moving notes *inside* a trusted repository keeps it trusted. Turn the
switch off at any time to make agents ask again.

## Who should not use it

Anyone who can push to the repository can put text in front of your
agents. Do not trust a repository with outside contributors, a fork of
someone else's project, or a repository whose push access you don't
control.
