pages.title: Usage on this device
pages.description: Lumen counts starts, commands and errors on your device only. The weekly report is off until you turn it on, and you send it yourself. Nothing leaves without your click.
pages.md:
Lumen has no analytics and no tracking. To know whether the app is used and
what breaks, it keeps a few **counters on your device**. They never leave
it unless you send them yourself.

## What is counted

Per day, in the browser's local storage (`lumen.usage.v1`):

| Counter | What it holds |
|---|---|
| Starts | how many times the app opened |
| Commands | how many times each command ran, by its id from the app's code (`file.exportHtml`, `help.feedback` …) |
| Errors | how many uncaught errors happened: one number, no message, no stack, no file |

The counters hold no note text, no file names, no user or device id and no
time of day. A counter name has to look like a command id: no spaces, no
slashes, no runs of digits or capitals. Anything you typed can't become one.
Commands named after something in your vault are counted under one fixed
name each: every installed template as `template.apply`, every recent file
as `recent.open`, every plugin command as `plugin.command`. So a template
called after a source never shows its name.
The last 60 days are kept.

## The dashboard

**Help: Usage on this device** in the command palette shows:

- the day you started using Lumen
- how many of the last 7 and 30 days you used it
- whether you came back after a week and after a month
- the most used commands, and how many commands went unused for 30 days

There you can turn counting off, which also clears the counts, or clear them
at any time.

## The weekly report: only when you send it

The dialog shows the whole report as JSON, exactly as it would be sent. It
holds counts only: the app version, the week, days used, retention, starts,
errors, the 20 most used commands of the app, and the number of unused ones.

- **Open on GitHub** opens a new tab with a GitHub issue form that has the
  report in it. Nothing is sent until you submit that form yourself. The
  click is listed in the [privacy ledger](/ai/privacy/) with its size.
- **Copy** puts the JSON on the clipboard.
- **Remind me once a week** is off by default. When you turn it on, a
  notice appears once a week with a button that opens the dialog. The notice
  sends nothing.

Without one of these clicks, Lumen makes no request for usage. The tests
check this (`src/__tests__/usageMetrics.test.ts`): counting, errors, the
dashboard and the report make 0 requests and add 0 ledger entries. A report
built after secrets were planted in the vault's storage contains none of
them.

pages.title: Vault encryption at rest
pages.description: Encrypt the whole vault where it is stored — OPFS, a real folder or the desktop folder — with a passphrase, a recovery key and auto-lock.
pages.md:
Optional. **Command palette → Vault encryption…** encrypts every note and
file of the vault where it is stored, so a copied browser profile, a lost
laptop or a synced folder shows only ciphertext. Lumen asks for the
passphrase when it opens the vault.

> **Read this before you turn it on.** An encrypted vault can't be read as
> plain text by Obsidian, git, a text editor or any other program — only by
> Lumen with the passphrase or the recovery key. If you use the same folder
> with other tools, keep the vault unencrypted (or keep a plain export).

## What is encrypted

| Where | How |
|---|---|
| Every file of the vault — notes, attachments, canvases, `.trash/`, `.git/` | AES-256-GCM, one random nonce per write, on every storage: the browser's own storage (OPFS), a real folder you picked in the browser, the desktop app's folder |
| History snapshots (the backups the Version History panel shows) | AES-256-GCM in IndexedDB |
| Agent traces (the last 50 runs, which include parts of notes) | AES-256-GCM in IndexedDB; migrated when encryption is turned on, deleted when it is turned off |
| Semantic search index (embeddings and the text of each chunk) | AES-256-GCM in IndexedDB |
| The search index's saved copy (the notes' text, so a large vault reopens fast) | AES-256-GCM and an HMAC-SHA256 signature in IndexedDB, written and checked in the index worker with keys of its own; a copy that was changed is refused and the vault is read in full |
| AI answer cache | Not written while the vault is encrypted; emptied when encryption is turned on or off |
| The open note and the open tabs, which Lumen normally keeps in `localStorage` to resume a session | Not kept; after a reload you open the notes again from the vault |

The fast search index lives in memory. Its saved copy is sealed with two
keys derived from the vault's key for this one job (HKDF-SHA256), bound to
the vault and the copy's format, and signed; the worker that writes it never
sees the vault's key. While the vault is locked nothing is written, and
the copy waits for the next unlock.

**Not encrypted:** file and folder names, file sizes and dates (the vault
stays a normal folder of files); the list of recent files; API keys and
tokens (they have their own store, see [Secrets and encryption](/security/vault/));
the encrypted sync's own state; version history of live collaboration rooms;
results of batch AI jobs; what the learning critic remembers. A vault export
(zip or folder) is plain text on purpose.

## Passphrase, recovery key, lock

- **Passphrase** — at least 12 characters. The key is derived with
  **Argon2id** (RFC 9106), memory-hard so guessing on graphics cards is
  slow. Lumen picks the most memory this device opens within a second:
  46 MiB in one pass, or 19 MiB in two on a slower device (OWASP's
  options). It runs in Lumen's own code, with no extra library, and is
  checked against the RFC's test vectors. A vault made before this, with
  PBKDF2-SHA256 (600,000 iterations), still opens and stays on PBKDF2,
  including when you change the passphrase. To move it, choose **Switch to
  Argon2id** under Vault encryption. Update Lumen on every device that
  opens the vault first: an older Lumen refuses an Argon2id vault (it
  doesn't misread it), so Lumen never switches on its own. Only the small
  header file is rewritten.
- **Recovery key** — 30 characters (150 random bits), shown **once**, when
  you turn encryption on, before anything is encrypted. Lumen goes on only
  after you confirm you saved it. The vault's key is derived from it, so it
  opens the vault even if you forget the passphrase *and* even if the
  vault's encryption header files were lost. Case, spaces and dashes don't
  matter when you type it back.
- **Lock** — after 15 minutes without a key press or a click (choose 5, 15,
  30, 60 minutes or never in the dialog), or **Lock now**. A locked vault
  covers the app with the unlock screen; nothing is read or written until it
  is unlocked, and saves made meanwhile go on afterwards.
- **Change passphrase** re-wraps the key; no file is re-encrypted.

## Safety: what happens if something goes wrong

- **Wrong passphrase** — refused; nothing is read or written.
- **Turning it on or off is cut off** (tab closed, battery, crash) — each
  file is converted copy-first: the new version is written next to it,
  read back and checked, and only then replaces the file. Every file is
  always either complete plain text or complete ciphertext, and Lumen reads
  both. **Check and repair** finishes the job.
- **A file changed by another program meanwhile** is left alone and done by
  the next run. A file that doesn't decrypt with this vault's key is
  reported and never overwritten or deleted.
- **The header** (`.lumen-encryption.json`, plus `.lumen-encryption.backup.json`)
  is written twice; one damaged copy is fine. It is removed only when no
  encrypted file is left. If both are gone, the recovery key brings the
  vault back.
- **A plain file dropped into the folder** reads normally and is encrypted
  by Check and repair.
- An encrypted vault can't be **moved** to another place (the move would
  copy decrypted notes): turn encryption off, move, turn it on again.

## Turning it off

**Vault encryption… → Turn off encryption** asks for the passphrase again,
then decrypts every file back to plain text. History comes back in the clear;
agent traces and the semantic index are deleted (they are rebuilt).

pages.title: Secrets and encryption
pages.description: How Lumen stores API keys and tokens, and how to encrypt a document.
pages.md:
Lumen keeps the secrets it needs — AI provider keys, Git and cloud tokens,
the collaboration room password, the research search key — out of plain
browser storage. The whole vault can also be encrypted with a passphrase and
a recovery key — see [Vault encryption at rest](/security/vault-encryption/);
the secrets described here are kept apart from it.

## Where secrets live

| Where Lumen runs | How secrets are stored |
|---|---|
| Browser / installed web app | Each secret is encrypted with AES-GCM-256 under a WebCrypto key that is **non-extractable**: no script can read out the raw key bytes. The secrets no longer sit in localStorage as plain text, so a glance in DevTools, a localStorage dump or a synced settings export shows only ciphertext. |
| Desktop app on macOS / Windows | The operating system's keychain (Keychain / Credential Manager). Lumen keeps only the secret names, so it knows what to load. |
| Old engines without IndexedDB or WebCrypto | Plain localStorage, as before. Lumen reports this mode instead of hiding it. |

**Honest limits:**

- The key is stored in the same IndexedDB database as the encrypted
  secrets, and Lumen decrypts them at startup without asking for a
  password. Someone who copies the whole browser profile and opens it in
  Lumen can therefore use the stored key and read the secrets.
  Non-extractable stops the key from being *exported*, not from being
  *used*. Protecting against a copied profile needs a password you type
  (planned with whole-vault encryption, task 11.4) or the desktop app's
  OS keychain.
- Code running inside Lumen's own origin could also ask WebCrypto to
  decrypt. The Content Security Policy and the HTML sanitizer are what
  keep foreign code out.

Plain-text secrets left by older versions are encrypted and moved at startup.

## Encrypting a document

`⌘K → 🔒 Encrypt Document` encrypts the open note with AES-256-GCM under a
password you type. The note is replaced by an encrypted block; `Decrypt
Document` restores it. Lumen does not keep the password — lose it and the
note cannot be recovered.

## What is not encrypted

Your notes themselves are plain Markdown files (in the browser's private
file system, or a folder on desktop). Encrypting the whole vault at rest is
an option, with **🔐 Vault encryption…**: see
[Vault encryption at rest](/security/vault-encryption/).

pages.title: CI on Buildkite, without GitHub Actions
pages.description: Buildkite Free schedules lumen-md's gates on our own machines (the verification factory's host and a Mac) and posts a commit status for every gate on every PR, plus a signed receipt.
pages.md:
Lumen doesn't use GitHub Actions. The verification factory
([its page](/self-hosting/verification-factory/)) tests the `verify/*` heads
every night, but a PR itself showed no ✓ or ✗. Plan W7.21 adds that:
**Buildkite Free** schedules the jobs, and our own agents run them:

- the factory's Ubuntu host runs every job in Playwright's own image (Docker)
- Tal's Mac runs **WebKit on macOS** on every build (queue `mac`)

Each gate posts its own GitHub commit status (`lumen/buildkite: <gate>`), and
the last job seals a **receipt** in the factory's format.

## What runs

`.buildkite/pipeline.yml` is generated from `.github/workflows/ci.yml`. The
gates are not typed twice: each Buildkite job runs the exact `run:` text of
ci.yml's steps.

| Job | ci.yml steps | Queue |
|---|---|---|
| `static` | typecheck, hygiene, headers, docs sync, plan, hard-coded strings, DoD, unused files, docs complete, i18n drift (all run, then it fails if any failed) | linux |
| `lint`, `licenses` | ESLint with its baseline; the licence gate | linux |
| `build` | build with the canary secrets, both secret scans, the bundle budget | linux |
| `vitest` ×4, `vitest-merge` | the whole suite in 4 shards balanced by time, merged, with ci.yml's 65% coverage gate | linux |
| `e2e-chromium`, `e2e-firefox` | every spec (Firefox under xvfb with software GL, as on GitHub) | linux |
| `e2e-webkit` | every spec, on macOS | **mac** |
| `e2e-prod`, `e2e-headers`, `local-ai`, `ocr-cer` | as in ci.yml | linux |
| `lighthouse` | main and PRs labelled `lighthouse` only, as in ci.yml | linux |
| `receipt` | the signed receipt, after every gate (pass or fail) | linux |

The steps ci.yml has that are not gates (installs, PR comments, the
main-only size cache, diagnostics) are listed with a reason in
`NOT_GATES` in `scripts/buildkite/lib.mjs`.

**No gate can go missing.** `npm run ci:pipeline` fails when:

- ci.yml has a step that the pipeline neither runs nor lists with a reason
- a step was renamed, or the e2e matrix gained a browser
- the committed `pipeline.yml` is not what ci.yml gives
- a job has `soft_fail`, or retries on a test failure (only a lost agent is retried)
- WebKit is off the Mac's queue, or skipped
- a gate posts no status, or the receipt doesn't wait for it

After changing ci.yml: `npm run ci:pipeline -- --write` and commit the file.

### Shards by time

`vitest --shard` splits by file count, so one shard can get all the slow files.
`vitest-plan` packs the files by their last measured time instead (longest
first, each to the lightest shard). The times come from the previous merge,
kept on the host. The first run packs by file size. `vitest-merge` fails
when:

- a planned file did not run, or ran twice
- a shard report is missing
- one of the suites the offline harnesses skip did not run or failed

The receipt records the actual spread between the longest and the shortest
shard.

### Why builds are started by the host, not by GitHub's webhook

Every commit and PR title here carries `[skip ci]` (that keeps GitHub Actions
off). Buildkite skips a build whose commit message or PR title contains
`[skip ci]`, `[ci skip]`, `[skip-ci]` or `[ci-skip]` ([Buildkite: skipping
builds](https://buildkite.com/docs/pipelines/skipping)). So the factory host
runs `scripts/buildkite/trigger.mjs` every 5 minutes (a systemd timer). It
creates a build through Buildkite's REST API for each new head of an open PR
from this repository, with a message without the marker.

- Heads from forks are never built: their code would run on our machines.
- A commit that already has a build is never queued again.
- PRs untouched since the timer started are left alone. Add them with `--backfill N`.

## Free tier (checked 14.11.2026 on buildkite.com/pricing)

- Up to 5 users and **up to 10 concurrent jobs on self-hosted agents**
- 2,000 hosted Linux minutes a month (we use none: our agents are self-hosted)
- 30-day build and artifact retention (the receipts live in `lumen-md-receipts`, so they outlast it)
- $0, no credit card

Commit statuses come from Buildkite's GitHub app. Its "Limited Access"
variant has no code access but can write commit statuses
([Buildkite: GitHub](https://buildkite.com/docs/pipelines/source-control/github)).
Our agents clone the public repository themselves.

## Owner setup (once, about 20 minutes)

1. Sign up at buildkite.com (the Free plan). Note the organization slug.
2. **Settings → Repository Providers → GitHub (Limited Access)**: install
   it on `talstilkol/lumen-md` only.
3. **Agents → the default cluster → Queues**: create two self-hosted queues,
   `linux` and `mac`. Under **Agent tokens**, create one token.
4. **Pipelines → New pipeline** `lumen-md`:
   - repository `https://github.com/talstilkol/lumen-md.git`
   - steps: `buildkite-agent pipeline upload`, on queue `linux`
   - under GitHub settings, leave **Update commit statuses** unticked: the
     pipeline sets its own statuses
   - don't add the GitHub webhook: those builds would be skipped anyway, and
     the host starts the builds
5. **Personal settings → API Access Tokens**: a token for this organization
   with **read_builds** and **write_builds** only.
6. The factory host (after its own setup, from the factory's page) and the Mac:

```bash
# on the Mac, with the factory host in VM=ubuntu@<ip>
printf 'Agent token: '; read -rs AGENT; echo; printf 'API token: '; read -rs API; echo
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/talstilkol/lumen-md/ci/buildkite/scripts/buildkite/agent-bootstrap.sh -o /tmp/bk.sh
scp /tmp/bk.sh "$VM":/tmp/
printf '%s\n%s\n' "$AGENT" "$API" | ssh "$VM" 'sudo bash /tmp/bk.sh --secrets-stdin --org <org-slug>'
printf '%s\n' "$AGENT" | bash /tmp/bk.sh --secrets-stdin      # this Mac: queue mac
unset AGENT API
```

The script reads the tokens from stdin, never from the command line, and
stores them with mode 0600. The agent:

- runs as the factory's user
- clones only lumen-md (`allowed-repositories`)
- runs no plugins and no hooks from the checkout

`--dry-run` prints every action without changing anything. On the Mac, the
agent runs in your login session (a LaunchAgent), so the Mac must be logged
in and awake for `e2e-webkit` to run.

## Checking it

- `npm run ci:selftest`: the generated commands run through `run.sh`, with
  Docker, npm and the agent emulated. It also covers the shard plan on the
  real test files, the receipt (sealed, checked, a changed byte rejected),
  the trigger against local API stand-ins, and the bootstrap into a
  temporary root.
- `node scripts/buildkite/receipt.mjs --verify <receipt.json> --key keys/<host>.pem`:
  checks a receipt from a build or from `lumen-md-receipts`.

pages.title: Moving production to another host
pages.description: The runbook for moving Lumen's production from Vercel Hobby to Cloudflare Pages in under an hour, before the first payment. It covers the new address, the users' notes that stay with the old one, the redirect, the checks and the way back.
pages.md:
Vercel's Hobby plan is for **non-commercial use only**
([fair-use guidelines](https://vercel.com/docs/limits/fair-use-guidelines)).
Lumen takes its first payment with the paid relay (plan W5.25). Before that,
production must move to a host that allows commercial use, or Vercel must
be upgraded to Pro ($20 a seat a month). This page is the move. It takes
about 45 minutes and can be undone in 5 (plan W6.9).

**The gate.** `deploy/hosting.json` names the production host and its plan.
`npm run hosting:gate` fails any build that takes payments while production
is on a plan without commercial use. It runs first in every Vercel build
(`scripts/vercel-build.mjs`) and in `pages:deploy`. The payment variables are
`VITE_BILLING_ENDPOINT`, `VITE_ENTITLEMENT_ENDPOINT`, the price IDs, and
`LUMEN_COMMERCIAL=1`. So the first payment cannot ship on Hobby by accident.

## Why the address changes

`lumen-md.vercel.app` belongs to Vercel. Its DNS can't point anywhere else.
The new production address is therefore a new free one:
**`https://lumen-md.pages.dev`**, Cloudflare's subdomain for the Pages
project. A custom domain can be added later, the same way (Cloudflare
dashboard → the project → Custom domains). That makes a third move, so pick
the domain before users have notes on `pages.dev`, if you can.

## The users' notes stay with the old address

Lumen is local-first. The notes live in this browser's storage **for one
address** (OPFS and IndexedDB are per origin). A browser opening
`lumen-md.pages.dev` starts empty, even if it used `lumen-md.vercel.app`
yesterday. A plain redirect would hide everyone's notes. So the old address
keeps serving the app, built with `VITE_MOVED_TO`
(`src/pwa/hostMoveBoot.ts`), and it does two things:

- **A browser that never used the app there** (empty `localStorage`, checked
  before the app starts) goes straight to the same path, query and hash on
  the new address.
- **A browser with notes there** keeps the app and gets a banner (English
  and Hebrew). It downloads every note and attachment as one `.zip` (the vault
  export), then opens the new address, where the user imports the file
  (Import vault). Sync and Git users can instead connect the same provider
  again at the new address.

The old address keeps no payment code (the gate enforces this), so it stays
within Hobby's terms. It just hands people over.

## The move (about 45 minutes)

On the Mac, in the repository, from `main`:

```sh
# 1. Once: the Cloudflare account and project (5 min)
npx wrangler@4 login
npx wrangler@4 pages project create lumen-md --production-branch main

# 2. The same commit on both hosts, checked (10 min)
git checkout main && git pull && npm ci
npm run pages:deploy -- --prod        # hosting gate, build, pages:check --prepare, host parity, upload
npm run hosts:parity -- --live https://lumen-md.vercel.app https://lumen-md.pages.dev
```

The live parity must end with `0 failing`. Its one accepted difference is
`/missing-image.png`: Vercel answers 404, Pages answers the app (see
`ACCEPTED` in `scripts/lib/hostParity.mjs`). Open the new address. Check the
editor, the PDF reader and a playground block (its runner page has its own
policy), and look for `Content-Security-Policy` errors in the console.

```sh
# 3. Make the new host production (5 min)
#    deploy/hosting.json: "production": "cloudflare-pages"; commit it to main.
#    Payments are allowed from this commit on (on the Pages build only).

# 4. The old address hands over (Vercel dashboard → lumen-md → Settings →
#    Environment Variables, Production) (10 min)
#    VITE_MOVED_TO = https://lumen-md.pages.dev
#    then redeploy main on Vercel. No payment variables there, ever.

# 5. Check the handover (5 min)
#    A private window on https://lumen-md.vercel.app/notes/x → lands on
#    https://lumen-md.pages.dev/notes/x. A normal window that has notes →
#    the banner; "Download my notes" saves a .zip; import it on pages.dev.
```

Then update the address everywhere it is written: the README, the store
listings, `public/sitemap.xml`, `og:url` in `index.html`, and the OAuth
redirect URIs of the sync providers (Google, Dropbox, GitHub). The OAuth
providers check the exact origin, so sign-in fails at the new address until
it is added.

## The way back (5 minutes)

Clear `VITE_MOVED_TO` on Vercel and redeploy. Set `"production": "vercel"`
in `deploy/hosting.json` again. Nothing is deleted at either step. Notes a
user made on `pages.dev` in the meantime stay there; the banner flow works in
the other direction too (build the Pages copy with
`VITE_MOVED_TO=https://lumen-md.vercel.app`).

## Drill: under an hour

The acceptance of W6.9 is a timed drill: steps 2 to 5 on a branch
deployment (`npm run pages:deploy` without `--prod`, and a Vercel preview
with `VITE_MOVED_TO` set for that branch only). Write down the minutes per
step in the PR of the drill.

pages.title: Self-hosting with Docker
pages.description: Run Lumen on your own infrastructure with the docker-compose bundle.
pages.md:
> Lumen is a **local-first** editor — by default everything runs inside
> your browser, no servers needed. This guide is for teams who want to
> own the persistence layer (collab, billing, audit log) on their own
> infrastructure.

## What's in the bundle

`docker-compose.yml` brings up five services on a single VM:

| Service | Port | What |
|---|---|---|
| `lumen-web` | 80 | nginx serving the React SPA + strict CSP — the same image as the Fly deployment (`Dockerfile`, `deploy/nginx.conf`) |
| `lumen-signal` | 4444 | y-webrtc signaling — peers find each other |
| `lumen-collab` | 4445 | Persistent Hocuspocus server (SQLite + backups on the `collab-data` volume; health: `/healthz`) |
| `lumen-billing` | 4446 | Stripe webhook handler (optional) |
| `postgres` | 5432 | Entitlements + audit log (collab does **not** write here — a Postgres snapshot archive is not implemented) |

A collab volume (`collab-data`: SQLite + its own hourly backups) and a Postgres volume (`postgres-data`)
persist outside container lifecycles.

## Prerequisites

- A Linux VM with **2 vCPU + 4 GB RAM** (Hetzner CX22, DigitalOcean
  basic-2, AWS t4g.medium are all fine)
- **Docker 24+** and **Docker Compose v2**
- A domain pointing at the VM (we'll use `lumen.example.com` below)

## 5-minute install

```bash
# 1. Clone Lumen
git clone https://github.com/talstilkol/lumen-md.git
cd lumen-md

# 2. Copy + edit the env template
cp .env.onprem.example .env.onprem
$EDITOR .env.onprem
#   set LUMEN_PG_PASSWORD to a strong value
#   set LUMEN_BASE_URL to your domain
#   leave LUMEN_COLLAB_TOKEN empty for now (see the note below)
#   leave Stripe / Sentry / WorkOS empty for now

# 3. Build + start
make onprem-up
```

After ~60 s of image build + container start, visit
`http://<vm-ip>` and you should see the Lumen editor.

:::caution[`LUMEN_COLLAB_TOKEN` in this bundle]
The bundle passes `LUMEN_COLLAB_TOKEN` to the collab server, but not to the
app it builds (the root `Dockerfile` has no `VITE_YJS_WEBSOCKET_TOKEN`
argument), and the app has no screen for entering one yet. With a token
set, the app's own clients are refused by the collab server. Keep it
empty, or build the web image yourself with `VITE_YJS_WEBSOCKET_TOKEN`
(see [Persistent rooms](/collab/persistent/)). New rooms are end-to-end
encrypted either way.
:::

## DNS setup (recommended)

Point these subdomains at the VM:

```
lumen.example.com    A    <vm-ip>
signal.example.com   A    <vm-ip>   # or proxy via lumen-web
collab.example.com   A    <vm-ip>
```

Then put a TLS terminator (Caddy, Cloudflare Tunnel, or your existing
nginx) in front. The bundled nginx serves HTTP only; the ports are
mapped 1:1 so a reverse proxy can terminate SSL upstream.

Serve Lumen from the root of its own (sub)domain, as above. The
security headers that ship with the app (the bundled nginx config,
`public/_headers` and `deploy/vercel.base.json`) match root paths. If you build with
a sub-path `base` such as `/app/`, prefix those routes yourself,
including the Web Playground's `/playground-runner.html`, `/assets/*`
and `/playground/*` rules. Without them the playground preview is blocked.

Every host runs the Web Playground, including Netlify (an edge function
gives the runner page its own headers there). What works where, and the
`LUMEN_RUNTIMES=slim` option for a smaller image, are in
[Where Lumen runs](/self-hosting/hosting/).

## Optional: Billing

If you want to gate Pro features (persistent collab, semantic search,
fine-tune AI) behind a paywall, add Stripe credentials and re-up with
the `billing` profile:

```bash
# In .env.onprem
STRIPE_SECRET_KEY=sk_live_xxx
STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET=whsec_xxx

# Bring up with the billing service
docker compose --env-file .env.onprem --profile billing up -d
```

The billing worker runs `wrangler local-mode` so the same code that
powers the Cloudflare deployment also runs in your VM.

## Optional: Sentry telemetry

Build the web image with `--build-arg VITE_SENTRY_DSN=https://<key>@<host>/<project>`
(Sentry or a self-hosted GlitchTip) to make error reports available. They
stay **off** until a user turns them on with the Telemetry pill in the status
bar; note text, titles and paths are removed first, and each report is listed
in the privacy ledger. The DSN's host is added to the CSP at build time. A DSN
is public by design, not a secret. See [Monitoring and web vitals](/security/monitoring/).

## Optional: SSO with WorkOS

Set `WORKOS_API_KEY=…` and `WORKOS_CLIENT_ID=…` to enable SAML / OIDC
sign-in. A workspace admin pastes their IdP metadata URL into Settings
→ Organisation; WorkOS handles the protocol dance.

## Daily ops

| What | Command |
|---|---|
| Tail logs | `make onprem-logs` |
| Restart everything | `make onprem-down && make onprem-up` |
| Check Postgres | `docker compose exec postgres psql -U lumen` |
| Hard reset (deletes all data) | `make onprem-reset` |

## Backup

The two Docker volumes are the only state Lumen owns:

```bash
# Postgres dump
docker compose exec postgres pg_dump -U lumen lumen | gzip > lumen-pg-$(date +%F).sql.gz

# Collab volume (collab.sqlite and backups/; the server also keeps hourly backups itself)
docker run --rm -v lumen_collab-data:/data -v "$(pwd)":/backup alpine \
  tar czf /backup/lumen-collab-$(date +%F).tar.gz -C /data .
```

User documents themselves never leave the browser — they live in OPFS
(Origin Private File System) per browser, per origin. Encourage users
to back up their local content with `⌘K → Export the whole vault…`
(see [Export and import](/workspace/export-import/)).

## Updating Lumen

```bash
git pull
make onprem-up   # rebuilds images + restarts containers
```

Database migrations run automatically on container start
(`docker/postgres-init.sql` is idempotent).

## Sizing for scale

Single-VM 2 vCPU / 4 GB handles:

- Up to ~50 concurrent collab rooms (LevelDB hot cache)
- ~1k entitlement reads / sec
- Linear cost on audit volume — every mutation writes one row

For larger deployments, split:

- `lumen-web` + `lumen-signal` on one VM (stateless, horizontally
  scalable)
- `lumen-collab` on a dedicated VM with a persistent EBS / Block-Storage
  volume
- Postgres on managed RDS / Cloud SQL

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Likely cause |
|---|---|
| 502 from `lumen.example.com` | reverse proxy can't reach `lumen-web:80` |
| Editor loads but collab silently fails | `lumen-signal` not reachable; check WS upgrade rules in proxy |
| Pro features stay locked | `lumen-billing` not in the compose profile, or webhook signature secret wrong |
| `pg_isready` fails | `LUMEN_PG_PASSWORD` mismatch between `.env.onprem` and the volume |

If something else breaks, `make onprem-logs` is your friend — the
five-line per-service prefix makes it easy to spot the offender.

The bundle passes LUMEN COLLAB TOKEN to the collab server, but not to the app it builds (the root Dockerfile has no VITE YJS WEBSOCKET TOKEN argument), and the app has no screen for entering one yet. With a token set, the app's own clients are refused by the collab server. Keep it empty, or build the web image yourself with VITE YJS WEBSOCKET TOKEN (see Persistent rooms). New rooms are end-to-end encrypted either way.

sections.heading: DNS setup (recommended)
sections.text: Point these subdomains at the VM: Then put a TLS terminator (Caddy, Cloudflare Tunnel, or your existing nginx) in front. The bundled nginx serves HTTP only; the ports are mapped 1:1 so a reverse proxy can terminate SSL upstream. Serve Lumen from the root of its own (sub)domain, as above. The security headers that ship with the app (the bundled nginx config, public/ headers and deploy/vercel.base.json) match root paths. If you build with a sub-path base such as /app/, prefix those routes yourself, including the Web Playground's /playground-runner.html, /assets/ and /playground/ rules. Without them the playground preview is blocked. Every host runs the Web Playground, including Netlify (an edge function gives the runner page its own headers there). What works where, and the LUMEN RUNTIMES=slim option for a smaller image, are in Where Lumen runs.

sections.heading: Optional: Billing
sections.text: If you want to gate Pro features (persistent collab, semantic search, fine-tune AI) behind a paywall, add Stripe credentials and re-up with the billing profile: The billing worker runs wrangler local-mode so the same code that powers the Cloudflare deployment also runs in your VM.

sections.heading: Optional: Sentry telemetry
sections.text: Build the web image with --build-arg VITE SENTRY DSN=https:// @ / (Sentry or a self-hosted GlitchTip) to make error reports available. They stay off until a user turns them on with the Telemetry pill in the status bar; note text, titles and paths are removed first, and each report is listed in the privacy ledger. The DSN's host is added to the CSP at build time. A DSN is public by design, not a secret. See Monitoring and web vitals.

sections.heading: Optional: SSO with WorkOS
sections.text: Set WORKOS API KEY=… and WORKOS CLIENT ID=… to enable SAML / OIDC sign-in. A workspace admin pastes their IdP metadata URL into Settings → Organisation; WorkOS handles the protocol dance.

sections.heading: Daily ops
sections.text: What Command --- --- Tail logs make onprem-logs Restart everything make onprem-down && make onprem-up Check Postgres docker compose exec postgres psql -U lumen Hard reset (deletes all data) make onprem-reset

sections.heading: Backup
sections.text: The two Docker volumes are the only state Lumen owns: User documents themselves never leave the browser — they live in OPFS (Origin Private File System) per browser, per origin. Encourage users to back up their local content with ⌘K → Export the whole vault… (see Export and import).

sections.heading: Updating Lumen
sections.text: Database migrations run automatically on container start (docker/postgres-init.sql is idempotent).

sections.heading: Sizing for scale
sections.text: Single-VM 2 vCPU / 4 GB handles: Up to 50 concurrent collab rooms (LevelDB hot cache) 1k entitlement reads / sec Linear cost on audit volume — every mutation writes one row For larger deployments, split: lumen-web + lumen-signal on one VM (stateless, horizontally scalable) lumen-collab on a dedicated VM with a persistent EBS / Block-Storage volume Postgres on managed RDS / Cloud SQL

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: Symptom Likely cause --- --- 502 from lumen.example.com reverse proxy can't reach lumen-web:80 Editor loads but collab silently fails lumen-signal not reachable; check WS upgrade rules in proxy Pro features stay locked lumen-billing not in the compose profile, or webhook signature secret wrong pg isready fails LUMEN PG PASSWORD mismatch between .env.onprem and the volume If something else breaks, make onprem-logs is your friend — the five-line per-service prefix makes it easy to spot the offender.

pages.title: Where Lumen runs
pages.description: What works on which host — Cloudflare Pages, Netlify, Vercel and the Docker image — and how each one is configured.
pages.md:
Lumen is a static app: `npm run build` produces `dist/`, and any host that
serves files can run it. Each host still has to do three things right: send
the security headers of `security/policy.json` (the app's strict
Content-Security-Policy, and the *different* policy of the two runner pages
that the Web Playground and live-js blocks open in a sandboxed frame), serve
the same-origin WebAssembly runtimes, and know the deployment's own endpoint
origins. The table is checked by `src/__tests__/hosting.test.ts` against the
configuration files, so it cannot drift from them.

## What works where

| Capability | Cloudflare Pages | Netlify | Vercel | Docker image (compose, Fly) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| The editor under the full policy (response header + `<meta>`) | ✅ `_headers` | ✅ `_headers` | ✅ `vercel.ts` | ✅ `deploy/nginx.conf` |
| Deep links (SPA routes) | ✅ | ✅ `netlify.toml` redirect | ✅ rewrite | ✅ `try_files` |
| Web Playground (sandboxed runner, own policy, framed by the app) | ✅ `! Header` detaches the catch-all | ✅ edge function `runner-headers` | ✅ excluded from the catch-all | ✅ own `location` |
| live-js runner | ✅ | ✅ edge function | ✅ | ✅ |
| Workers that need eval (Graphviz, Ruby, TypeScript checker, webR) with their own policy | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| On-device OCR (tesseract.js worker policy) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Same-origin WebAssembly runtimes (Python, Ruby, ONNX Runtime, the dictation VAD model, OCR; ≈100 MB). R (webR, GPL-3.0) is not in the build: each user downloads it from an R block, or the operator stages it with `npm run webr:local` | ✅ in `dist/` | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ `LUMEN_RUNTIMES=full` (default) · `slim` drops them |
| Your endpoint origins in `connect-src` (`VITE_*_ENDPOINT`) | ✅ at build time | ✅ at build time | ✅ `vercel.ts` at build time | ✅ build args → nginx |
| HSTS | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | — the TLS terminator in front sends it |
| Cross-origin isolation (COOP / COEP, multi-threaded WebAssembly) | — | — | — | ✅ (decision 15.10(7) whether it stays) |

Everything above the HSTS row works on every host. The last two rows are
deliberate differences, explained in `docs/security/headers.md`.

## One image

The compose bundle and the Fly deployment build the same `Dockerfile`:
nginx with `deploy/nginx.conf`, listening on 8080 as a non-root user
(`docker-compose.yml` maps it to port 80). Until plan 13.2 there were two
Dockerfiles with two different nginx configurations.

Build arguments:

| Argument | Default | What |
|---|---|---|
| `VITE_*_ENDPOINT`, `VITE_*_URL`, `VITE_CSP_CONNECT_EXTRA` | empty | The deployment's own services; added to `connect-src` in the header and the `<meta>` policy |
| `LUMEN_RUNTIMES` | `full` | `slim` removes the same-origin WebAssembly runtimes (≈100 MB measured on 24.10.2026: Pyodide 13.6, ruby.wasm 30.6, ONNX Runtime 41.2, tesseract.js 11.8, plus the 2.3 MB Silero VAD model; webR is never in the image, see live R below). The live-python and live-ruby blocks, OCR and local transcription then report that their runtime is not installed; everything else, the Web Playground, plugins and the canvas fonts included, is unchanged |

```bash
# the full image (compose: make onprem-up; Fly: fly deploy)
docker build -t lumen .
# a smaller one without the WebAssembly runtimes
docker build -t lumen --build-arg LUMEN_RUNTIMES=slim .
```

## Netlify

Netlify applies `dist/_headers` to every response and cannot detach the
catch-all rules the way Cloudflare's `! Header` lines do, so the two runner
pages used to inherit the app's `X-Frame-Options: DENY` and CSP, and the Web
Playground could not run there. `netlify/edge-functions/runner-headers.ts`
runs for `/playground-runner.html` and `/livejs-runner.html` only, drops the
frame denial and sets the runner's policy. Its policy strings are rendered
from `security/policy.json`: `npm run headers` fails when they drift.

## Live R (webR)

webR's binaries (R, libgfortran) are GPL-3.0, so no Lumen build or image
contains them. The first Run of a `live-r` block on a device offers the
download: the licence and the source come first, the files come from
webR's own CDN (`webr.r-wasm.org`, or the npm package on `cdn.jsdelivr.net`),
each one is checked against the checksums in the build's
`runtimes/webr.json`, and the service worker then serves them from this
origin, offline included. Both hosts are in `connect-src` for that download
only. An operator who accepts distributing webR under GPL-3.0 can serve it
instead: `npm run webr:local` before `npm run build` stages it in
`public/webr/`, and the R block then uses it without asking.

## The content frame's own site

Images, video and audio from other sites, embeds and Gists render, after you
allow them, inside Lumen's **content frame**. Since plan W6.40 that frame runs
on a separate site, `https://lumen-md-frame.pages.dev/`. Code in the frame
can't read the app's storage (your notes, keys and settings) or its pages,
even if a future bug let a page inject a script into the frame. The frame site
holds only two static files. What the frame shows travels in the URL's
`#fragment`, and browsers never send that to a server.

A deployment chooses its frame site when it builds:

```bash
# the official frame site (two static files; any static host on another site works)
node scripts/content-frame-site.mjs
npx wrangler pages deploy dist-frame --project-name lumen-md-frame
# the app, built to use it
VITE_CONTENT_FRAME_URL=https://lumen-md-frame.pages.dev/ npm run build
```

If you host your own frame site, add its origin to `frame-src` in
`security/policy.json` (route `app`) and the origins of your app to the
frame site's `frame-ancestors` (host `content-frame-site`). Then run
`npm run headers:write`.

A build without `VITE_CONTENT_FRAME_URL` still shows images, video, audio
and Gists in a frame that has no origin at all, so nothing in it can reach
the app. Embeds such as YouTube or Vimeo need an origin of their own to play,
so in that build they appear as a link that opens the player in a new tab.

pages.title: Android and iOS builds
pages.description: How the Android APK and iOS IPA are built on every pull request, what is unsigned until the store accounts exist, and which secrets sign them.
pages.md:
Lumen's mobile apps are the same web build wrapped by Capacitor: `android/`
and `ios/App/` are committed project skeletons, `npx cap sync` copies
`dist/` into them. `.github/workflows/mobile.yml` builds both on every pull
request, so a change that breaks the native projects shows up before it
merges.

## One command on your own machine (plan W4.22)

GitHub Actions are off in this repository (the owner's decision, 9.11), so
the mobile builds also run as one local command each. The workflow below is
kept for when Actions are on.

```bash
npm run mobile:check                                   # what is missing for each platform, and the fix
npm run mobile:android -- --version 0.2.0-beta.1       # signed AAB + signed APK + debug APK → release/mobile/
npm run mobile:ios -- --version 0.2.0-beta.1           # on a Mac: archive, upload, TestFlight
```

Both commands start with a preflight. It lists every missing tool, key or
setting with the exact command that fixes it, and stops before building.
`--dry-run` prints the commands without running them. `--version` defaults to
`package.json`.

**Build numbers.** Both stores need a number that grows on every upload. It
comes from the version: major·10⁶ + minor·10⁴ + patch·10² + the beta number
(99 for the release). For example, 0.2.0-beta.1 → 20001, 0.2.0-beta.2 → 20002,
and 0.2.0 → 20099. Android gets it as `versionCode`. iOS gets it as
`CURRENT_PROJECT_VERSION`, with `MARKETING_VERSION` set to 0.2.0, because iOS
takes no `-beta` in the version.

### Android

1. The web build (`VITE_LUMEN_CHANNEL=beta` for a beta), then `npx cap sync android`.
2. Gradle runs `assembleDebug bundleRelease assembleRelease` with `-PversionCode` / `-PversionName`.
3. Checks: the AAB is checked with `jarsigner` and the APK with `apksigner`. A
   bundle signed with the debug key (`CN=Android Debug`) is refused, because
   Play would reject it.
4. Output: `release/mobile/lumen-<v>.aab` (for Play), `lumen-<v>.apk`
   (sideloading), `lumen-<v>-debug.apk` (emulator and Firebase Test Lab), and
   `SHA256SUMS`.

Needs: JDK 21, the Android SDK with `platforms;android-36` (`ANDROID_HOME`),
and the upload keystore in `ANDROID_KEYSTORE_PATH`, `ANDROID_KEYSTORE_PASSWORD`,
`ANDROID_KEY_ALIAS` and `ANDROID_KEY_PASSWORD`. You make the keystore once:

```bash
keytool -genkeypair -v -keystore ~/.lumen-android/upload.jks -alias lumen -keyalg RSA -keysize 4096 -validity 10000
```

Keep it and its password in your password manager. With Play App Signing,
Google holds the app key and this is only the upload key, so a lost one can
be replaced. The first AAB has to be uploaded in the Play Console
(*Testing → Internal testing*). `--unsigned` builds only the debug APK, with
no keystore.

### iOS → TestFlight

1. The web build, then `npx cap sync ios`.
2. `xcodebuild archive` runs with **automatic signing through the App Store
   Connect API key** (`-allowProvisioningUpdates -authenticationKeyPath …`), so
   Xcode makes or reuses the distribution certificate and profile. There is no
   `.p12` and no profile to export by hand.
3. `xcodebuild -exportArchive` runs with an `exportOptions.plist` made for the
   build (method `app-store-connect`, destination `upload`). It uploads to App
   Store Connect. A beta is marked for internal testing only.
4. App Store Connect processes the build in 10–30 minutes. It then appears in
   **TestFlight → Internal Testing** for the team.

`--altool` exports the `.ipa` and uploads it with
`xcrun altool --upload-app … --apiKey --apiIssuer` instead. Apple marks
`--upload-app` as deprecated in favour of `--upload-package`, but it still
works. `--no-upload` only leaves `release/mobile/lumen-<v>.ipa`.

Needs: a Mac with Xcode 16 or newer, plus `APPLE_TEAM_ID`, `ASC_KEY_ID` and
`ASC_ISSUER_ID`. It also needs the key file: `ASC_KEY_PATH` points to
`AuthKey_<id>.p8`, or `ASC_KEY` holds its text. Make the key in App Store
Connect → Users and Access → Integrations → App Store Connect API, with the
**Admin** role, so Xcode may manage certificates. The `.p8` can be downloaded
only once. The app record (`com.lumen.editor`) must exist in App Store
Connect. Until `ITSAppUsesNonExemptEncryption` is set in `Info.plist` (see
`store/SUBMISSION.md`), App Store Connect asks the export-compliance question
for each build.

### Without a Mac or an Android SDK: Codemagic

`codemagic.yaml` runs the same two commands on Codemagic's macOS M2 machines.
It has no `triggering:` section, so nothing builds on a push. You start each
build by hand in the Codemagic UI. On 12.11.2026, Codemagic's pricing page
said a **personal account gets 500 free macOS M2 minutes a month**, reset on
the 1st. It also said there are no free minutes on Linux or Windows, and no
free minutes for Teams. So both workflows use the Mac, and an iOS build of
about 15–25 minutes fits many times a month. The environment groups
`lumen_ios` and `lumen_android` hold the same variables as above (the
keystore as `ANDROID_KEYSTORE_BASE64`). Check the current terms at
docs.codemagic.io/billing/pricing before relying on them.

### Smoke tests without a phone

- **Android:** a Firebase Test Lab robo run of the debug APK
  (`gcloud firebase test android run --type robo --app release/mobile/lumen-<v>-debug.apk --device model=<id>,version=<api>`).
  It is free on the Spark plan (see *Owner sessions* 1.6), or you can use an
  emulator from Android Studio.
- **iOS:** TestFlight on Tal's device, or BrowserStack App Live with the
  `.ipa` (open-source plan).

## What every pull request produces

| Job | Runner | Artifact | Signed? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Android APK | `ubuntu-24.04`, Temurin 21, Android SDK 36 | `lumen-android`: `app-debug.apk` (debug key, installable on a developer device) and `app-release-unsigned.apk` | debug: yes (debug key) · release: only with the keystore secrets |
| iOS IPA | `macos-14`, Xcode | `lumen-ios`: `Lumen-unsigned.ipa` | only with the certificate and profile secrets |

Without the store accounts (plan 15.7) both jobs stay green and the
artifacts are unsigned: they prove that the native projects compile against
the current web build. An unsigned IPA installs nowhere; the debug APK
installs on any Android device with developer mode.

Locally: `npm run android:open` / `npm run ios:open` build the web app, sync
it into the native project and open Android Studio / Xcode.

## Signing (optional secrets)

Set these repository secrets and the same jobs sign the release artifacts;
the release pipeline (plan 13.4) then publishes them.

| Secret | What |
|---|---|
| `ANDROID_KEYSTORE_BASE64` | The release keystore, base64 (`base64 -w0 release.keystore`) |
| `ANDROID_KEYSTORE_PASSWORD` | Its password |
| `ANDROID_KEY_ALIAS` | The key alias inside it |
| `ANDROID_KEY_PASSWORD` | The key's password |
| `IOS_CERTIFICATE_P12_BASE64` | The distribution certificate with its private key, as a `.p12`, base64 |
| `IOS_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD` | The `.p12` password |
| `IOS_PROVISIONING_PROFILE_BASE64` | The App Store provisioning profile for `com.lumen.editor`, base64 |
| `IOS_PROVISIONING_PROFILE_NAME` | Its name, as shown in the Apple developer portal |
| `APPLE_TEAM_ID` | The team identifier |

`android/app/build.gradle` reads the keystore from `ANDROID_KEYSTORE_PATH`
(the workflow decodes the secret there) and signs the release build only
when it is set; nothing in the repository holds key material. The iOS
export uses `ios/exportOptions.plist` (method `app-store-connect`) with the
team and profile filled in from the secrets.

Versions: `./gradlew -PversionCode=42 -PversionName=1.2.0` sets the Android
version; the iOS version is `MARKETING_VERSION` / `CURRENT_PROJECT_VERSION`
in the Xcode project. The release pipeline sets both from the tag.

## Safari and storage

Safari deletes a site's storage after seven days without a visit, and grants
`navigator.storage.persist()` only to installed apps. When the vault is not
persisted in Safari or in any iOS browser, and Lumen is not installed and not
the native app, a reminder shows once a week: export the vault, or add Lumen
to the Home Screen / Dock, where storage is kept. The native apps keep their
storage like any app.

pages.title: Native builds on free hosts
pages.description: How the desktop app, the Android AAB and the iOS IPA are really compiled without GitHub Actions — a Linux script for the second host, Codemagic's free macOS minutes, and a robo run on Firebase Test Lab or BrowserStack.
pages.md:
Plan W6.24. The native code (Rust in `src-tauri/`, Java in `android/`, Swift in
`ios/`) is compiled by its own toolchains — `cargo`, Gradle and Xcode — on
hosts that cost nothing. Nothing runs on a push: every build is started by hand.

## Desktop on Linux: `scripts/native/linux-build.sh`

On Ubuntu 24.04 (the verification factory's second host, a VM or a container):

```bash
bash scripts/native/linux-build.sh --install   # once: WebKitGTK headers, rustup, Node 22, JDK 21, Android SDK
bash scripts/native/linux-build.sh             # npm run build, cargo check --locked, cargo test, tauri build, Gradle
bash scripts/native/linux-build.sh --updater-bump   # also tauri-plugin-updater 2.14.1 (zip 9)
bash scripts/native/linux-build.sh --dry-run   # the commands only
```

- `cargo check --locked` refuses a `Cargo.lock` that does not match
  `Cargo.toml`; the script never updates the lock silently.
- `tauri::generate_context!()` embeds `dist/`, so the web build runs first.
- `--updater-bump` keeps the new lock only if `cargo check --locked` still passes.
- **Android needs x86-64.** Google ships no Android build tools for Linux on ARM
  ("Linux machines with ARM-based CPUs aren't currently supported",
  developer.android.com/studio/install). On the Oracle Ampere host the Gradle
  step is skipped and named; run it on x86-64, the Mac or Codemagic.
- The summary is written to `reports/native/<commit>.txt`.

## Phones and macOS: Codemagic

`codemagic.yaml` has these workflows (Codemagic → the app → Start new build):

| Workflow | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `mobile-release` | the signed AAB and the signed IPA from **one commit**; the AAB goes to Play's internal track, the IPA to TestFlight; `BUILD-INFO.txt` and `SHA256SUMS` name the commit |
| `android-robo` | the debug APK on Firebase Test Lab robo; with `LUMEN_SMOKE=browserstack`, the Espresso launch test on BrowserStack |
| `desktop-macos` | `cargo check --locked` and `tauri build` for macOS |
| `ios-testflight`, `android-aab` | one platform each (plan W4.22) |

The free tier (codemagic.io/pricing, checked 14.11.2026): 500 macOS M2 minutes
a month, one build at a time, 120 minutes per build, one user. Keys live in
Codemagic environment groups (`lumen_ios`, `lumen_android`, `lumen_play`,
`lumen_testlab`, `lumen_browserstack`) and are named in the repository, never stored.

## A robo run without a phone

```bash
npm run mobile:android -- --unsigned
FIREBASE_PROJECT=<id> bash scripts/mobile-device-smoke.sh testlab   # 2 virtual devices, Hebrew and English
bash scripts/mobile-device-smoke.sh testlab --physical              # 1 physical device
```

The devices are in `mobile/testlab/robo.yaml`. The no-cost Spark plan allows
10 virtual and 5 physical runs a day. **Firebase Test Lab shuts down on
30 September 2027** (firebase.google.com/docs/test-lab/usage-quotas-pricing),
so the fallback is BrowserStack App Automate:

```bash
(cd android && ./gradlew assembleDebugAndroidTest)
BROWSERSTACK_USERNAME=… BROWSERSTACK_ACCESS_KEY=… bash scripts/mobile-device-smoke.sh browserstack
```

It runs `LaunchSmokeTest` (the app starts and its WebView loads to 100 %) on two
real Android phones. BrowserStack's free trial includes 100 App Automate minutes.

pages.title: Performance gate
pages.description: npm run perf:gate measures FCP, LCP, TBT, TTI and CLS of a production build in Chromium, on desktop and a throttled phone, and fails on the error thresholds, without GitHub Actions.
pages.md:
The gate (plan 8.3) checks that a build loads fast enough before it ships.
It runs on your machine or against a preview deployment. GitHub Actions
are not needed.

```bash
npm run build && npm run perf:gate            # serves dist/ with vite preview
npm run perf:gate -- --url https://<preview>.vercel.app
```

## What it measures

Lighthouse CI is not in the lockfile, so the gate measures the same
numbers itself, with Playwright and Chromium's own performance entries:

- **FCP**: first contentful paint.
- **LCP**: largest contentful paint.
- **CLS**: layout shifts not caused by input.
- **TBT**: for each long task after FCP, the time beyond 50 ms, as
  Lighthouse counts it.
- **TTI**: the end of the last long task before a quiet window.
- The time until the editor takes input, reported as well.

Every load is cold: a fresh browser context, with no cache, no storage
and no service worker. There are 5 loads per profile, and the gate
reports the **median run**: the single load closest to the median FCP
and TTI. This matches Lighthouse's `median-run`, not its optimistic
default.

| Profile | Emulation |
|---|---|
| desktop | 1350 × 940, no throttling |
| mobile | Pixel 7, CPU 4× slower, 150 ms latency, 1.6 Mbps down |

## Thresholds

The thresholds are in `perf-gate.config.json`:

- **`error`** fails the gate (exit code 1).
- **`warn`** is reported.
- **`target`** is the plan's goal, shown next to the result until the
  runner meets it.

Desktop errors at the runner level set by decision 15.16 (20)/(21): FCP
1200 ms and LCP 3500 ms, with targets of 1000 ms and 2500 ms. Plans 8.1
and 8.2 tighten them. The mobile profile only warns until it has been
measured on the runner.

## Options

| Option | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--url <url>` | Measure a running server or deployment instead of `vite preview` |
| `--profiles desktop` | Only these profiles |
| `--runs 3` | Loads per profile (default 5) |
| `--out gate.md` | Write the Markdown summary, for a PR comment |
| `--json gate.json` | All runs, every metric |

`npm run lighthouse` (LHCI) still works when you install it with `npx`.
The gate does not depend on it.

pages.title: A second host and tests without Vercel
pages.description: Why Cloudflare Pages is Lumen's second host next to Vercel Hobby, what each free tier allows, how to deploy the same build there, what to do when a quota runs out, and how to run the whole test pipeline in Docker.
pages.md:
Vercel's Hobby plan builds every branch, one build at a time, 100
deployments a day, and is for **non-commercial, personal use only**. In
November 2026 its usage limit and one build slot held Lumen's checks up for
weeks. This page records the decision for a second host and a way to test
without any host (plan W4.27).

## The free tiers, compared

Checked on 12 November 2026 against each provider's own pages.

| | Vercel Hobby | Cloudflare Pages Free | Netlify Free | GitHub Pages |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Commercial use | ✗ personal, non-commercial only | ✓¹ | ✓¹ | ✗ not for running a business or SaaS |
| Builds | 100 deployments/day, 1 at a time | 500 builds/month, 1 at a time, 20 min each; **Direct Upload uses none** | 300 credits/month, a production deploy costs 15 (≈ 20/month); previews and branch deploys 0 | 10/hour (soft), 10 min each |
| Traffic | 100 GB, 1 M requests | not metered | 20 credits per GB, 2 per 10,000 requests, from the same 300 | 100 GB/month (soft), 1 GB site |
| Per file / files | — | 25 MiB per file, 20,000 files | — | — |
| Custom headers (CSP, runner pages) | ✓ `vercel.json` | ✓ `_headers`, with `! Header` to detach | ✓ `_headers` + an edge function for the runners | ✗ none: the CSP falls back to `<meta>`, no `frame-ancestors`, HSTS from GitHub only |
| Over the limit | features stop for 30 days | builds stop; the site stays up | **every site is paused** ("Site not available") until next month | warnings, then possible suspension |
| Without GitHub Actions | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✗ branch publishing runs a `pages-build-deployment` workflow |
| Monthly cost | $0 (Pro: $20 per developer seat) | $0 | $0 | $0 |

¹ No restriction on the provider's plan and limits pages, and a third-party comparison (hostfleet.pages.dev, April 2026) lists both as allowed; the owner should still read the terms of service before relying on it.

Sources: vercel.com/docs/plans/hobby, developers.cloudflare.com/pages/platform/limits,
docs.netlify.com (billing for credit-based plans, "How credits work"),
docs.github.com/pages (GitHub Pages limits).

## The decision: Cloudflare Pages, by Direct Upload

- **Cloudflare Pages** is the second host. Its traffic is not metered, the site
  stays up when a quota runs out, commercial use is allowed, and
  `public/_headers` is already written in its grammar: the runner pages detach
  the app's policy with `! Content-Security-Policy`, so the Web Playground and
  live-js work there without an edge function.
- **Direct Upload** (`npm run pages:deploy`): the build runs on your machine,
  so it uses none of Cloudflare's 500 builds and none of Vercel's 100
  deployments. Connecting the repository in the Cloudflare dashboard is
  optional; it gives a second build slot for branches (build command
  `npm run build && npm run pages:check -- --prepare`, output `dist`,
  `NODE_VERSION=22`).
- **Not Netlify** for a mirror: running out of credits pauses every site, and
  20 production deploys a month is too few. `netlify.toml` stays for anyone
  who self-hosts there.
- **Not GitHub Pages**: no custom headers (the CSP would lose
  `frame-ancestors` and the runner pages their own policy) and its publishing
  runs on GitHub Actions, which this project does not use.
- **Vercel Pro ($20 a month)** removes the 100-a-day limit and is required
  anyway once Lumen is used commercially. That is the owner's decision; the
  second host does not depend on it.

### One limit to know: 25 MiB per file

`ruby+stdlib.wasm` (ruby.wasm, about 30.6 MB) is larger than Cloudflare's
25 MiB per file. `npm run pages:check` reports every such file;
`--prepare` (which `pages:deploy` uses) removes them from that upload
and lists them in `dist/pages-dropped.json`. On the Cloudflare copy, live-ruby
blocks then say their runtime is not installed — like the Docker image's
`slim` variant. Everything else is the same build.

## Deploy the same build

```bash
npx wrangler@4 login                                   # once
npx wrangler@4 pages project create lumen-md --production-branch main   # once
npm run pages:deploy                    # a preview named after the current branch
npm run pages:deploy -- --prod          # production: https://lumen-md.pages.dev
```

Each deployment carries the commit hash. To check that both hosts serve the
same build of a commit, compare the entry chunk's content hash (Vite names
it after its content):

```bash
for h in https://lumen-md.vercel.app https://lumen-md.pages.dev; do
  curl -s "$h/" | grep -o 'assets/index-[A-Za-z0-9_-]*\.js'
done
```

The two lines are equal when both builds had the same `VITE_*` settings.

## When a quota runs out

| What ran out | What to do |
|---|---|
| Vercel deployments (100 a day) or usage (30-day pause) | Previews: `npm run pages:deploy` from the branch. Checks: `npm run ci:docker`. Production stays on the last Vercel deployment; switch traffic to `lumen-md.pages.dev` only if Vercel stops serving it. |
| Cloudflare builds (500 a month, Git integration only) | Keep using Direct Upload, which does not count. |
| Both hosts unavailable | The Docker image (`docker build -t lumen .`, see [Where Lumen runs](/self-hosting/hosting/)) serves the same app anywhere. |

## The test pipeline in Docker

When no host can build, run everything the Vercel preview build runs, on your
machine, with no GitHub Actions:

```bash
npm run ci:docker                         # every ci:local step, e2e on Chromium
npm run ci:docker -- --only typecheck,test
npm run ci:docker -- --skip e2e
```

`Dockerfile.ci` starts from Playwright's own image for the exact
`@playwright/test` version in `package-lock.json`, so the browsers match and
nothing is downloaded during the tests. It installs with `npm ci`, copies the
checkout (git history included: `Dockerfile.ci.dockerignore`) and runs
`npm run ci:local`. The log and the Playwright report land in
`ci-docker-out/`. It works with Podman too: `DOCKER=podman npm run ci:docker`.

## Production-ready on both hosts

The same build serves the same headers and routes on both hosts (plan W6.9).
`npm run hosts:parity` emulates each host from its own configuration and
compares 17 probe paths; `pages:deploy` runs it on the real `dist/` before
every upload. Three Cloudflare details it covers:

- **2,000 characters a line.** Cloudflare skips a longer `_headers` line
  without failing the deploy. The app policy is therefore two lines that
  the host joins into two policies, enforced together as exactly one.
- **`/x.html` answers 308 to `/x`.** The runner pages have rules at both
  paths.
- **A missing chunk is a 404.** `pages:check --prepare` writes
  `assets/404.html`, so a chunk of the previous deploy is not answered with
  the app's HTML.

Moving production between hosts: [the cut-over runbook](/self-hosting/cut-over/).

pages.title: The verification factory
pages.description: A free second machine that runs every test of every verify/* head each night in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit, signs a receipt per commit and posts the result to GitHub as commit statuses, without GitHub Actions.
pages.md:
Lumen doesn't use GitHub Actions, and until now every real check depended on
one rented build slot (Vercel Hobby) and a sandbox that is blocked until
December. The verification factory (plan W6.5) is a machine of our own that
does the full run every night:

- the whole vitest suite in 2 shards, the slow nightly-only suites included
- every e2e spec on **chromium, firefox and webkit**, 4 shards each
- the data-safety drill (#470, its `drill:data-safety` script) and `cargo check` of the
  desktop shell, when the commit has them; the mutation run on Sundays
- the suites the offline harnesses can't run (`e2eeUi`, `pdfReader`,
  `dictationLocal`, `vaultEncryption`): the receipt names each one, and
  vitest fails if any of them did not run

Each head of `verify/*` gets one **sealed receipt** for its exact commit, in
the public repository `talstilkol/lumen-md-receipts`, and one GitHub commit
status per suite (`lumen/factory: e2e webkit`, …) that links to it. A head
that hasn't changed since its last run gets a heartbeat that names the
receipt of that same commit. Evidence is never carried over to another
commit. Every Sunday unchanged heads run again, to catch flaky tests.

## The host: Oracle Cloud Always Free, Ampere A1

Checked on 12 November 2026 against each provider's own pages.

| | What it gives for $0 | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **Oracle Cloud Always Free, Ampere A1** | 1,500 OCPU hours and 9,000 GB hours a month = **2 OCPUs (arm64) and 12 GB**, always on; 200 GB block storage; 10 TB a month outbound | **Chosen.** A permanent Ubuntu 24.04 VM with no time limit. Playwright publishes its Docker image for arm64, with all three browsers. |
| Buildkite Free | up to 5 users, **10 concurrent jobs on our own agents**, 2,000 hosted Linux vCPU minutes a month, 30 days retention | A scheduler, not a machine: its agents still need a host. It can be added later on top of this one (plan W7.21). 2,000 hosted minutes is about 66 minutes a night, less than one full run. |
| Tal's Mac (launchd) | whatever the Mac has | **The fallback.** The same script installs a LaunchAgent; it runs only while the Mac is on. |
| GitLab for Open Source | Ultimate with 50,000 compute minutes | Not chosen: needs an application, a GitLab group, a yearly renewal, and the namespace "can't seek to make a profit". |
| GitHub Actions | — | The owner's rule: not used. |

**Terms to know:**

- Oracle halved the Always Free Ampere allowance in June 2026, from 4 OCPUs
  and 24 GB to 2 OCPUs and 12 GB. Some guides still quote the old figures.
- Oracle reclaims an Always Free VM that is idle over 7 days: 95th-percentile
  CPU under 20%, network under 20% and, on A1, memory under 20%. A nightly
  run of about two hours keeps the CPU's 95th percentile above that.
- The Always Free Ampere shape lives only in the account's **home region**,
  which is chosen at sign-up and can't be changed. Popular regions often
  answer "Out of host capacity". Try another availability domain, or try
  again later.
- Stay on the Always Free tenancy. Upgrading to Pay As You Go protects the VM
  from reclamation, but anything above the free allowance is then billed.

Sources: docs.oracle.com/iaas/Content/FreeTier/resourceref.htm (Always Free
resources, idle reclamation), linuxiac.com (the June 2026 change),
buildkite.com/pricing, about.gitlab.com/solutions/open-source/join,
playwright.dev/docs/intro (Ubuntu 22.04/24.04/26.04 on x86-64 or arm64) and
Playwright's `utils/docker/publish_docker.sh` (images for amd64 and arm64).

**Speed, an estimate, not yet measured:** with 2 OCPUs, the full e2e run in
three browsers (about 330 tests each) is projected at 90–110 minutes. The
plan's target is under 60. If the first nights confirm that estimate, move
one browser to the Mac (`LUMEN_FACTORY_HOST=mac`, its own key), or add
Buildkite agents (W7.21).

## The owner's one step (about 25 minutes, once)

**In the browser:**

1. Sign up at Oracle Cloud (cloud.oracle.com, "Start for free"). It asks for
   a card to check your identity; Always Free resources are not charged.
2. *Compute → Instances → Create instance*: image **Canonical Ubuntu 24.04
   (aarch64)**, shape **VM.Standard.A1.Flex** with **2 OCPUs and 12 GB**,
   boot volume 100 GB, a public IPv4 address, and your `~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub`.
   Note its public IP.
3. GitHub → *Settings → Developer settings → Fine-grained tokens → Generate
   new token*: name `lumen-factory`, resource owner `talstilkol`, expiration
   1 year, **Only select repositories: talstilkol/lumen-md**, repository
   permission **Commit statuses: Read and write**. Nothing else. Copy the token.

**Then one paste in the Mac's terminal** (gh is already logged in there):

```bash
VM=ubuntu@<the VM's public IP>
gh repo create talstilkol/lumen-md-receipts --public --add-readme --description "Signed nightly test receipts of lumen-md (plan W6.5)"
ssh-keygen -q -t ed25519 -N "" -C lumen-factory -f /tmp/lumen-factory-key
gh repo deploy-key add /tmp/lumen-factory-key.pub --repo talstilkol/lumen-md-receipts --allow-write --title lumen-factory
printf 'Paste the github_pat_ token: '; read -rs TOKEN; echo
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/talstilkol/lumen-md/chore/verify-factory/scripts/factory/bootstrap.sh -o /tmp/lumen-bootstrap.sh
scp /tmp/lumen-bootstrap.sh "$VM":/tmp/
{ printf '%s\n' "$TOKEN"; cat /tmp/lumen-factory-key; } | ssh "$VM" 'sudo bash /tmp/lumen-bootstrap.sh --secrets-stdin --run-now'
rm -f /tmp/lumen-factory-key /tmp/lumen-factory-key.pub; unset TOKEN
```

Once the branch is merged, put `main` in place of `chore/verify-factory`
in the URL and pass `--branch main`.

The token and the key go over ssh's standard input, never as command-line
arguments. On the VM they are stored with mode 0600, readable only by the
`lumen` user. The deploy key can write to the receipts repository and
nothing else. The token can only post commit statuses to lumen-md. It can't
push code. That is why the receipts live in their own repository: a token
that can write receipts to lumen-md could also push to `main`, which has no
branch protection.

The bootstrap does the rest:

1. installs Docker (Ubuntu's `docker.io`), git, gh and Node 22
2. creates a `lumen` user, and on a 12 GB machine a 4 GB swap file
3. stores the token and the deploy key
4. clones the factory's code and the receipts repository, and creates the
   Ed25519 signing key (`~/.config/lumen-md/nightly-ed25519.pem`, mode 0600)
5. writes `/etc/lumen-factory/env`
6. installs a systemd timer for 01:17 Israel time. It is persistent, so a
   night missed while the VM was down runs at boot.
7. checks that the receipts remote answers, the token sees the repository,
   Docker runs, and the factory can plan a night

`--run-now` starts the first night right away. See it with
`journalctl -u lumen-factory -f`.

### On the Mac instead (the fallback)

Run the same script without sudo. Pipe in the same secrets:
`{ printf '%s\n' "$TOKEN"; cat /tmp/lumen-factory-key; } | bash /tmp/lumen-bootstrap.sh --secrets-stdin`.
On a Mac it checks for node, git and gh (`brew install node gh`). It runs the
steps natively, without Docker, and installs the LaunchAgent
`dev.lumen-md.factory`. launchd runs a night that was missed while the Mac
slept as soon as it wakes. The Mac signs with its own key, `keys/mac.pem`.

## What a night writes

In `talstilkol/lumen-md-receipts`:

| Path | What |
|---|---|
| `commits/<sha>/full-<time>.json` | the sealed receipt of one full run: every step with its exit code, duration, the sha256 of its output and its last lines; the result per suite; the must-run suites; the failing tests and the PR that last changed each failing file |
| `nights/<date>.json` | the sealed list of heads that night: ran, unchanged (with the receipt of the same commit), or left for later |
| `nights/<date>.md` | the morning report: what failed, from which PR, and what changed since the previous report of the same branch |
| `keys/<host>.pem` | the public half of each host's signing key |

Check a receipt anywhere:
`npm run nightly -- --verify commits/<sha>/full-….json`. The digest always
works. For the signature, copy that host's key to
`reports/nightly/PUBLIC_KEY.pem`. A changed number breaks both.

## Commands

```bash
npm run factory:run -- --dry-run            # list the heads and what would run tonight
npm run factory:run -- --only verify/train --rerun --max 1
npm run factory:run -- --no-push --no-status   # keep everything on this machine
npm run factory:selftest                    # the bootstrap and a whole night, with Docker, npm and gh emulated
```

The self-test runs the real bootstrap script and the real `run.mjs`,
signing and checking included, against local stand-in repositories. Docker,
npm, gh, systemd and launchd are small programs that record what they're
asked to do. So it shows that the scripts are wired correctly. It shows
nothing about the real image, browsers or test suite. Those run on the
first real night.

sections.heading: The verification factory
sections.text: Lumen doesn't use GitHub Actions, and until now every real check depended on one rented build slot (Vercel Hobby) and a sandbox that is blocked until December. The verification factory (plan W6.5) is a machine of our own that does the full run every night: the whole vitest suite in 2 shards, the slow nightly-only suites included every e2e spec on chromium, firefox and webkit , 4 shards each the data-safety drill (#470, its drill:data-safety script) and cargo check of the desktop shell, when the commit has them; the mutation run on Sundays the suites the offline harnesses can't run (e2eeUi, pdfReader, dictationLocal, vaultEncryption): the receipt names each one, and vitest fails if any of them did not run Each head of verify/ gets one sealed receipt for its exact commit, in the public repository talstilkol/lumen-md-receipts, and one GitHub commit status per suite (lumen/factory: e2e webkit, …) that links to it. A head that hasn't changed since its last run gets a heartbeat that names the receipt of that same commit. Evidence is never carried over to another commit. Every Sunday unchanged heads run again, to catch flaky tests.
